subject: rla
title: Inference and Textual Evidence
objectives: You will tell the difference between information a text states directly (explicit) and information it suggests (implicit).
You will make reasonable inferences by combining text clues with everyday knowledge, and state them in your own words.
You will choose the textual evidence that best supports an inference or claim, using the checks relevant, specific, and direct.
You will infer a character's feelings, motives, and meaning from speech, actions, thoughts, and the reactions of others.
You will recognize the four inference traps: overreach, outside knowledge, contradicted, and true but irrelevant.

slides.title: Inference and Textual Evidence
slides.board:
Week 2 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Tell what a text states from what it suggests
  • Make inferences with text clues + what you know
  • Choose the evidence that best proves a point
  • Read characters' feelings and motives
  • Spot the four inference traps

Plan: Warm-up · Learn and practice together · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Last week was about what a text says: its main idea and the details that support it. This week is about what a text means but does not say outright. Questions that use the words infer, suggest, imply, and most likely are some of the most common on the RLA test, and many are paired with a second question asking which evidence proves your answer. By the end of the hour, you should be able to make an inference and then put your finger on the exact words that prove it.
ask: When a friend texts “Fine.” with a period and nothing else, what do you think they mean? How do you know? (expected: they are probably not fine; the short reply and the period are clues. Build on this: that is an inference.)

slides.title: Week 1 review: quick fire
slides.board:
Answer out loud.

  1. Topic or main idea? “Rising grocery prices”
  2. A paragraph opens, “Many people think renting is wasted money. However, …” Where is the main idea most likely?
  3. A paragraph covers bike lanes' effects on safety, commute times, and local shops. Which trap is the answer “Bike lanes make streets safer”?
  4. Name two things a good summary leaves out.
steps: 1. Topic. It is a phrase. It cannot be true or false.
2. Right after “However.” The first sentence is a belief the author is about to push back on.
3. Too narrow. Safety is one of three effects; the main idea must cover all three.
4. Opinions (yours or anyone's added) and minor details such as small numbers, names, and examples.

notes.say: This warm-up reviews last week's lesson, because today's skill sits right on top of it. You cannot infer what a text suggests until you know what it says. Give the student about a minute per question, and ask for a reason with every answer. If any of these is shaky, make a note: the same moves come back in today's practice.
notes.answer: 1. Topic. 2. In the sentence after “However,” where the author's real point begins. 3. Too narrow. 4. Personal opinions and minor details (also accept: anything not in the text, and copied sentences).
notes.watch: If the student calls question 1 a main idea because it “sounds like a headline,” replay the true-or-false test: “Can ‘rising grocery prices’ be true or false?” It cannot, so it is a topic.

slides.title: Week 1 review: one paragraph
slides.board:
Twenty years ago, the Elm Street lot was a fenced square of weeds and broken glass. Today it holds forty garden beds, a tool shed, and a waiting list of families who want a plot. Volunteers give about a third of each harvest to the food pantry next door. On summer evenings, neighbors who once never spoke trade recipes over the fence.

  1. Is the main idea stated or implied?
  2. State the main idea in one sentence.
  3. Which detail best supports “The garden helps people who do not garden there”?
steps: 1. Implied. No single sentence covers the change, the pantry, and the neighbors.
2. Sample: “The Elm Street lot has become a community garden that feeds and connects the neighborhood.”
3. A third of each harvest goes to the food pantry. The pantry serves people outside the garden.
Today's bridge: in question 1 you figured out something the text never said. That is an inference.

notes.say: Read the paragraph aloud once. This is last week's skill, but question 1 is the bridge to today. No sentence says the main idea, so the student has to build it from the details. That move, putting clues together to reach an idea the text never states, is exactly what an inference is. Say so when you reveal step 1.
notes.answer: 1. Implied. 2. Any sentence covering the change and its effects, such as “An empty lot became a garden that feeds and brings together the neighborhood.” 3. The food pantry detail. The waiting list shows demand from gardeners, and the recipe trading shows neighbors connecting, but only the pantry detail reaches people who do not garden there.
notes.watch: Students may pick the waiting list for question 3. Ask, “Who is on that list?” They are people who want to garden there, so the detail does not prove the claim about non-gardeners.

slides.title: Stated vs. implied
slides.board:
Stated (explicit)Implied (implicit)
What it isSaid in so many wordsShown through clues
Example“Dana was angry.”“Dana slammed the door so hard the pictures shook.”
GED wordingAccording to the passage…It can be inferred… The author suggests… most likely…

The writer implies. The reader infers.

notes.say: Some information is stated directly: the text says it in so many words. Other information is implied: the writer gives clues and trusts you to put them together. Both Dana sentences tell us she is angry, but only the first one says so. Draw an arrow on the board from writer to reader: the writer implies, the reader infers. The GED uses both verbs, and students mix them up, so say them together a few times.
ask: “Kim yawned through the whole meeting.” Is Kim's tiredness stated or implied? (expected: implied; the yawning is the clue)
Fill in: The author ___ that the plan will fail. The reader ___ that the plan will fail. (expected: implies; infers)
notes.watch: Students sometimes say “the author infers.” Correct it every time: authors imply (send the hint), readers infer (catch it).

slides.title: What happened here?
slides.board:
You walk into a kitchen. On the counter is half of a chocolate cake with the number 7 in blue frosting. Torn wrapping paper is stuffed into a trash bag by the door. Three balloons are tied to a chair, and a stack of frosting-smeared paper plates sits by the sink.

What happened? What can you NOT know?
steps: Clues: cake with a 7, torn wrapping paper, balloons, used plates.
Connect: I know these are the leftovers of a birthday party.
Inference: A seventh birthday party took place here recently.
Cannot know: the child's name, how many guests came, whether it was a surprise, whether everyone had fun.

notes.say: Model this one out loud. First collect the clues, then connect them, then say the conclusion in one sentence. The second list, what we cannot know, matters just as much as the first, because that is where wrong answer choices come from. A choice like “The party was a surprise” might be true, but nothing in the scene proves it.
ask: Could “The party was for a girl” be a correct answer? Why or why not? (expected: no; nothing in the scene says whether the child is a boy or a girl)

slides.title: The inference formula
slides.board:
Text clues + what I already know = inference

Text clueWhat I knowSo I can infer
Wet shoes, dripping umbrellaRain makes things wetIt is raining outside

Prove-it test: “Where does it say that, or which clues lead there?” No words to point to? Cross it out.

notes.say: An inference is not a guess. It is the conclusion the text leads a careful reader to. The clues must come from the text; everyday knowledge is only the glue that connects them. It never replaces them. Then teach the prove-it test: for every answer, the student must be able to point to the words. A correct inference is usually a short step from the text, not a long leap.
ask: A man walks in stamping snow off his boots. What can you infer? What is the clue, and what do you know? (expected: it is snowing or has snowed; clue: snow on boots; know: snow sticks to boots outside)
notes.watch: Watch for students who reverse the formula and start from what they know about the topic. Ask, “Would someone who knew nothing about this subject reach that answer from this text alone?”

slides.title: Inference from an informational text
slides.board:
“When the Harbor Street Clinic began offering evening hours, every appointment between 5 and 8 p.m. was booked within two days. Within a month, the share of patients who missed daytime appointments fell from 18 percent to 9 percent. Several patients said they could not afford to take unpaid time off for a checkup.”

What can you infer about why patients had been missing appointments?
steps: Clues: evening slots filled in two days; daytime no-shows were cut in half; patients cannot afford unpaid time off.
Connect: If no-shows dropped once evening hours opened, and patients named work as the problem, daytime work was keeping them away.
Inference: Many patients had missed daytime appointments because they had to be at work.
Prove it: the last sentence plus the drop from 18 to 9 percent.
Not supported: “The clinic will soon open every evening” (no plans are mentioned) and “All patients prefer evenings” (all goes too far).

notes.say: Walk through the four steps slowly: read the question, go back to the text, make your own inference before any choices, then prove it. The clinic paragraph never says “Patients missed appointments because of work,” but three clues point straight there.
ask: What does “booked within two days” tell you? (expected: there was strong demand for appointments after work hours)

slides.title: Infer it together
slides.board:
A. Sign on a café door: “Starting Monday, we will close at 3 p.m. instead of 8 p.m. We are sorry for the inconvenience. We are hiring! Ask at the counter.”

B. Pool notice: “Early-morning lap swim is canceled until we hire a second lifeguard.”

For each: What can you infer? Which words prove it?
steps: A. Clues: shorter hours + “We are hiring!” in the same notice.
A. Inference: The café is cutting hours because it does not have enough workers. “Going out of business” overreaches: a business that is hiring is not closing.
B. Clue: lap swim returns only when there is a second lifeguard.
B. Inference: The pool has only one lifeguard right now, which is not enough to run early lap swim.

notes.say: Now the student leads. For each sign, ask for the clues first, then the inference, then the proof. Reveal each step only after the student has answered it. On sign A, offer the trap choice “The café is going out of business” and have the student explain why it fails.
ask: Why does “We are hiring!” matter on a sign about shorter hours? (expected: it suggests the reason for the shorter hours: not enough staff)
Does sign B say how many lifeguards work there now? (expected: not directly; “a second lifeguard” implies there is one)
notes.answer: A: The café is shortening its hours because it is short on workers; proof: the hiring line in the same notice. B: The pool has only one lifeguard now and needs two for early lap swim; proof: “until we hire a second lifeguard.”
notes.watch: If the student answers sign A with “The café is losing customers,” ask for the words that prove it. There are none; the only reason the sign hints at is staffing.

slides.title: Choosing the best evidence
slides.board:
“Which detail best supports…?” Several choices will be on the topic. The best one passes three checks:

Relevantabout the exact claim, not just the same subject
Specifica fact, number, action, or quotation
Directif it is true, the claim must be true (or very nearly)

Paired questions: Part A asks for the inference; Part B asks for the evidence. The line that led you to Part A is usually Part B.

notes.say: Many GED reading questions come in pairs: first an inference, then “Which evidence best supports your answer?” Several choices will mention the right subject; the student has to find the one that actually proves the claim. Teach the three checks and the key test question: “If this detail is true, does the claim have to be true?” Weak evidence only makes a claim possible. Strong evidence makes it hard to deny.
ask: Claim: “The new bakery is popular.” Which is more direct: “The bakery opened in March” or “There is a line out the door every Saturday”? (expected: the line; the opening date says nothing about popularity)

slides.title: Which evidence is strongest?
slides.board:
Claim: “The town's free tax-help clinic is meeting a real need.”

A. The clinic meets in the basement of the public library.
B. Tax forms have become more complicated over the years.
C. Volunteers helped 412 residents file this year, and 90 more were still on the waiting list when the season ended.
D. The clinic's director has volunteered there for ten years.
steps: A: about the clinic, but says nothing about need. True but irrelevant.
B: general, not about this town. It only makes a need possible.
D: shows the director's dedication, not the community's need.
C: relevant (it measures demand), specific (412 and 90), direct (more people wanted help than the clinic could serve). Best evidence.

notes.say: Run the three checks on every choice out loud, and name the problem with each weak one. The point is not just to find C but to explain why the others fail, because on the test the wrong choices are written to look relevant.
ask: Which word in C is the strongest proof of need? (expected: the waiting list; people wanted help and could not get it)

slides.title: Evidence together: the pay-what-you-can shelf
slides.board:
Rosa Delgado placed a shelf by her bookstore door with a sign: “Pay what you can. Take what you need.” Her accountant warned she would lose money. By spring, however, the coffee can beside the shelf was collecting about as much each month as the books would have earned at regular prices. Regular customers began leaving bags of used books on the doorstep. This spring, Delgado added a second shelf.

  1. How has the shelf worked out?
  2. Which detail best shows the accountant was wrong?
steps: 1. Inference: The shelf has been a success.
1. Proof: the can collects about what the books would have earned, and she added a second shelf. People do not expand something that is failing.
2. Best evidence: “By spring, however, the coffee can … was collecting about as much each month as the books would have earned at regular prices.” It answers the exact prediction: losing money.

notes.say: Read the passage aloud, then let the student lead. For question 1, push for the proof as well as the answer. For question 2, point out the signal word however: it marks the sentence that answers the accountant's warning.
ask: Why is “Delgado added a second shelf” weaker evidence for question 2? (expected: it suggests success, but the accountant's warning was about money, and only the coffee can sentence is about money)
notes.answer: 1. It has been a success: the can brings in about regular prices, and she expanded. 2. The coffee can sentence; it directly contradicts the warning that she would lose money.
notes.watch: Students may choose the donated bags of books for question 2. Those show customer support, not money. Ask, “What exactly did the accountant predict?”

slides.title: Inferring about characters
slides.board:
Stories rarely say “she was nervous.” They show it. Four sources of clues:

Sayswords, tone, what is left unsaid
Doesactions, gestures, body language
Thinksthoughts the narrator shares
Others reacthow other characters treat them

People do not always mean exactly what they say. A joke, a short answer, or a silence can carry the meaning.

notes.say: Fiction writers show feelings instead of naming them. Teach the four sources of clues, and stress the last line on the board: characters, like real people, often say one thing and mean another. A gruff boss who jokes instead of praising is still praising. The student's everyday experience reading people is a real strength here; the job is to tie that reading to specific words.
ask: Your coworker says “Great. Just great.” after the printer jams. What does she mean? (expected: the opposite; she is frustrated)

slides.title: Reading a character: Marcus
slides.board:
“Marcus checked his phone for the fourth time in ten minutes. When the coffee shop door opened, he stood up so fast that his chair scraped the floor. Then he saw it was only the mail carrier, and he sat back down slowly and smoothed the front of his new shirt.”

What can you infer about Marcus?
steps: Phone four times in ten minutes → people check often when waiting → he is waiting for someone.
Jumps up, then sits slowly → disappointment slows people down → he expected a specific person.
Smooths his new shirt → people fuss over clothes before something that matters → the meeting is important to him.
Inference: Marcus is nervously waiting to meet someone who matters to him. We cannot know who.

notes.say: Fill in the three-column organizer one row at a time. Each row turns one action into a piece of the inference. Then ask what we cannot infer: who he is waiting for. A choice that names the person, such as “his new boss” or “a date,” would be overreach.
ask: Which clue shows he was let down? (expected: sitting back down slowly when it was only the mail carrier)

slides.title: What does he really mean?
slides.board:
“Mr. Ortiz looked at the dented fender, then at his teenage son, then back at the fender. ‘Well,’ he said, ‘I guess you found the mailbox.’”

Which inference is best supported?

A. Mr. Ortiz thinks the damage is funny and does not care.
B. The son hit a mailbox with the car, and Mr. Ortiz is making a dry joke about it.
C. The son always drives carelessly.
steps: What happened: the dented fender + “found the mailbox” → the son hit a mailbox with the car.
A: a joke does not mean he does not care. His long look back and forth suggests he is not pleased. Overreach.
C: one dent does not prove a pattern; always goes too far. Overreach.
B is best: it explains both the dent and the dry tone of the remark.

notes.say: Let the student work this one with you. First ask what literally happened, then what Mr. Ortiz means by his line. Then have the student name the problem with each wrong choice. This is the “people do not always mean what they say” rule in action.
ask: What is Mr. Ortiz doing with his eyes, and what does that suggest? (expected: looking from fender to son and back; he is connecting the damage to his son and taking it in)
notes.answer: B. A and C both overreach: A turns a dry joke into not caring, and C turns one accident into “always.”
notes.watch: Some students take the line literally and say the son was looking for a mailbox. Ask, “Why would someone say ‘found’ about something they hit?” Dry humor often says the mild thing to mean the serious one.

slides.title: The four inference traps
slides.board:
TrapWhat it looks like
OverreachGoes further than the clues; watch all, never, always, only, proves
Outside knowledgeMight be true in life, but this text does not support it
ContradictedThe text says or shows the opposite
True but irrelevantA real detail that does not answer the question asked

notes.say: Wrong answers on inference questions are not random. They are built from four kinds of mistakes. Once the student can name the trap, eliminating choices gets much faster and much more confident. Stress true but irrelevant: it is the hardest to cut, because the student can find those words in the passage.
ask: A choice says something you know is true from the news, but the passage never mentions it. Which trap? (expected: outside knowledge)
notes.watch: Extreme words are a warning sign, not an automatic wrong answer. If the text says “every appointment was booked,” a choice with “every” can be right. Always check against the text.

slides.title: Name the trap
slides.board:
“The Westfield library added Saturday hours in March. Since then, the number of visitors on weekends has doubled, and the most crowded room is the one with public computers. A librarian said many visitors use the computers to apply for jobs.”

What can be inferred? Name the trap in each wrong choice.

A. Many visitors come to the library to use its computers.
B. Every Westfield resident now visits on Saturdays.
C. Libraries are a good place to read quietly.
D. The Saturday hours have attracted few visitors.
steps: B: every resident? Visits doubled; that is not everyone. Overreach.
C: may be true in life, but the paragraph is about computers and jobs. Outside knowledge.
D: visits doubled. Contradicted.
A is correct: the computer room is the most crowded room, and a librarian says many visitors use the computers to apply for jobs.

notes.say: Work through each choice and say the trap name out loud before you cut it. Then prove the right answer with two clues. This is the habit you want on every inference question: no choice is cut without a reason.
ask: Write a true-but-irrelevant choice for this paragraph. (expected: any real detail that does not answer the question, such as “The Saturday hours began in March.”)

slides.title: What a line means, why a detail is there
slides.board:
“What does the speaker most likely mean?”

  1. Read the sentences just before and after the line.
  2. Ask: is this literal, or a figure of speech, joke, or exaggeration?
  3. Restate it in plain words that fit the context.

“Why does the author include…?”

  1. Ask what the detail does: shows a contrast, gives proof, sets up a problem, answers a worry.
  2. Look for signal words nearby: however, that is why, exactly why, instead.

notes.say: Two more inference question types show up constantly. The first asks what a line most likely means, which is an inference about words that are not literal. The answer always comes from the context around the line. The second asks why the author included a detail; the answer is about the detail's job in the passage, not just what it says. Sentences right before and after are the key evidence in both.
ask: A coach says, “That was a game to forget.” What does she most likely mean? (expected: the team played badly; she is not asking anyone to forget it)

slides.title: Why is this detail here?
slides.board:
(1) In 2017, a council member argued that most people would never return the tools they borrowed from the new tool library. (2) Last year the library made 4,850 loans. (3) Only 4 tools never came back. (4) “People treat the tools like they belong to a neighbor,” the founder said, “because they do.”

Why does the author include sentence 1?
steps: Sentence 1 states a worry: people will not return tools.
Sentences 2–3 give the result: 4,850 loans, only 4 lost.
Sentence 4 explains why people return the tools.
Purpose: sentence 1 sets up an early doubt so the evidence can show it was wrong.

notes.say: Model how to find a detail's job. The question is not what sentence 1 says; it is why it is there. Look at what comes after it. The numbers answer the council member's worry, so sentence 1 sets up a worry that the rest of the paragraph shows was wrong.
ask: Would “to prove that the council member was careless” be a good answer? (expected: no; that overreaches; the passage shows his prediction was wrong, not that he was careless)

slides.title: Your turn: infer and prove
slides.board:
1. “Kenji's lunch sat untouched on his desk while he typed, deleted, and retyped the same sentence of his report.” What can you infer?

2. Stated, inferred, or not supported? (a) Kenji is writing a report. (b) Kenji is struggling with the report. (c) Kenji's boss is angry with him.

3. Inference: “The repair shop has more work than it can handle.” Best evidence? (a) The shop opened in 2009. (b) Customers wait three weeks for an appointment, and the owner stopped taking new orders until January. (c) Car repairs can be expensive.
steps: 1. Kenji is stressed or stuck on the report and is too focused on it to eat. Clues: untouched lunch; typing, deleting, retyping the same sentence.
2. (a) stated; (b) inferred; (c) not supported.
3. (b): relevant, specific, and direct. (a) is true but irrelevant; (c) is general and not about this shop.

notes.say: Set a four-minute timer and stay quiet while the student works. When time is up, have the student give each answer with the words that prove it before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. He is struggling with or focused on the report and has not eaten. 2. (a) stated (“his report”); (b) inferred from deleting and retyping; (c) not supported, no boss appears. 3. (b).
notes.watch: On problem 2, students often call (c) an inference because stress at work “usually” comes from a boss. That is outside knowledge. Ask, “Where is the boss in the text?”

slides.title: Your turn: characters
slides.board:
1. “When the coach began reading the list of names, Ana stared at the floor and gripped the edge of the bench. When the coach reached the last name, Ana let out a long breath and grinned at her best friend.” What can you infer?

2. “Jada read the email twice. Then she printed it and taped it to the refrigerator, right next to her son's spelling test with the gold star.” What can you infer about the email? What can you NOT infer?
steps: 1. Ana was worried she would not make the team and was relieved when she learned she made it. Clues: stares at the floor and grips the bench (worry); long breath and grin (relief).
2. The email brought good news Jada is proud of: she reads it twice, prints it, and displays it next to another achievement.
2. Cannot infer what the news was (a new job? a school acceptance?). Naming it would be overreach.

notes.say: Three minutes on the timer. Ask the student to name which kind of character clue (says, does, thinks, others react) each inference comes from.
notes.answer: 1. Ana was anxious about making the team, then relieved when the coach finished the list and she knew she had made it. 2. The email held good news she is proud of; we cannot know exactly what the news was.
notes.watch: On problem 1, a student may say “Ana's name was last.” The text does not say that; it says she relaxed when the coach reached the last name. Accept “she made the team” and keep the inference at that level.

slides.title: Your turn: traps and meaning
slides.board:
“Three residents at the meeting spoke in favor of the new park.” Name the trap:

1. “Every resident supports the park.”

2. “Parks raise property values.”

3. “No one at the meeting liked the park.”

4. A worker says, “If this copier jams one more time, I'm moving to the moon.” What does she most likely mean?
steps: 1. Overreach: three residents are not every resident.
2. Outside knowledge: might be true, but the sentence says nothing about property values.
3. Contradicted: three people spoke in favor.
4. She is extremely frustrated with the copier. “Moving to the moon” is an exaggeration, not a plan.

notes.say: Three minutes. Have the student say the trap name and a one-sentence reason for each. Then check problem 4 for the difference between literal and intended meaning.
notes.answer: 1. Overreach. 2. Outside knowledge. 3. Contradicted. 4. She is fed up with the copier jamming.

slides.title: GED question: paired, Part A
slides.board:
“For eleven years, Rosa Delgado has run Second Chapter Books. Last fall she added a pay-what-you-can shelf. A bus driver named Curtis Bell said he had not bought a book since high school. ‘Now I read on my breaks,’ he said. ‘Some weeks I put in a dollar, and some weeks I put in five.’”

Part A. What can be inferred about Curtis Bell?

A. He cannot afford to buy books at regular prices.
B. The shelf helped him become a regular reader again.
C. He reads more than any other customer.
D. He was a strong reader in high school.
steps: A: we know only that his payment varies. Saying he cannot afford books is overreach.
C: no comparison with other customers appears. Not supported (overreach).
D: the passage says nothing about how well he read in high school. Not supported.
B is correct: no books since high school, and “Now I read on my breaks” shows the shelf turned him back into a reader.

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student predict an answer before looking at the choices, then eliminate one choice at a time, naming the trap. Keep the line they used as proof, because Part B is next.
ask: Before the choices: what changed for Curtis Bell? (expected: he started reading again because of the shelf)
notes.answer: B. A overreaches from “some weeks a dollar” to poverty; C and D have no support in the text.
notes.watch: A is the most tempting choice because it sounds kind and realistic. Ask, “Which words say he cannot afford books?” There are none.

slides.title: GED question: paired, Part B
slides.board:
Part B. Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

A. “For eleven years, Rosa Delgado has run Second Chapter Books.”
B. “Some weeks I put in a dollar, and some weeks I put in five.”
C. “A bus driver named Curtis Bell…”
D. “He had not bought a book since high school. … ‘Now I read on my breaks.’”
steps: A: about the store, not about Bell's reading. True but irrelevant.
B: about how he pays, not about whether he reads. It would support the overreach in Part A, choice A.
C: tells his job, nothing about reading.
D is correct: it shows the before (no books since high school) and the after (reading on breaks).

notes.say: Remind the student: the evidence for Part B is usually the line that led them to Part A. Eliminate with the three checks: relevant, specific, direct.
ask: Which Part A choice would the payment detail (B) have supported, if it were true? (expected: choice A, that he cannot afford books, which was the overreach)
notes.answer: D. It directly shows the change from not reading to reading regularly.

slides.title: GED question: character
slides.board:
“Teresa cut the key, smoothed one rough spot with a file, and handed it back. Mr. Haddad held both keys up to the window, then dropped the new one into his shirt pocket. He set a ring of four keys in front of her. ‘You open on Saturdays,’ he said. ‘The coffee maker's broken. Fix that and you can stay forever.’”

What does the coffee maker remark most likely suggest about Mr. Haddad?

A. He hired Teresa mainly to repair the store's equipment.
B. He is angry that no one has fixed the coffee maker.
C. He shows approval through dry humor instead of direct praise.
D. He doubts that Teresa will stay very long.
steps: A: he hands her the keys after she cuts a key; the coffee maker is a joke. Overreach.
B: nothing he says or does shows anger. Not supported.
D: “stay forever” and the store keys suggest the opposite. Contradicted.
C is correct: he never praises her in words; he pockets her key, gives her the store keys, and jokes. “Stay forever” over a coffee maker is a playful exaggeration.

notes.say: Ask the student to look at what Mr. Haddad does before deciding what his words mean. Then eliminate by trap.
ask: What two actions show he is pleased before he ever speaks? (expected: he pockets her key and hands her the store keys)
notes.answer: C. A overreaches, B is not supported, D is contradicted.
notes.watch: Literal readers pick A. Ask whether a boss would really hire someone “forever” over a coffee maker; the exaggeration signals a joke.

slides.title: GED strategy: Prove it before you pick it
slides.board:
1. Read the question; note who or what it asks about.
  2. Go to that part of the text and mark the clues.
  3. Predict the inference in your own words.
  4. Pick the closest choice and put your cursor on the words that prove it.
  5. Can't point to words? Cross the choice out and name the trap.

Paired questions: the line you pointed to in Part A is usually the answer to Part B.

notes.say: Inference choices are written to sound reasonable, so “that could be true” is never enough. The habit to build is simple: no answer is chosen until the student can point to the words. On paired questions this saves real time, because the work for Part A answers Part B. The same habit, point and prove, earns points on the extended response later in the course.
ask: What should you do if you like a choice but cannot find words that support it? (expected: cross it out; it is probably outside knowledge or overreach)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Writers do not tell you everything. A news story gives you numbers and quotations but lets you draw the conclusion. A story never says a character is scared; it shows her hands shaking. Figuring out what a text means but does not say is called making an inference. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, many questions ask what a passage suggests, what you can infer, or what a character would most likely do, and many come with a second question: which evidence best supports your answer? In this lesson you will learn to:

  • tell what a text states from what it implies
  • make inferences by combining text clues with what you already know
  • choose the evidence that best proves an idea
  • infer a character's feelings and motives
  • spot the four inference traps that make wrong answers sound right

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check. Answer it before you move on; if you miss it, you will see exactly why. Then go on to Practice and the Exit Check.

screens.title: Stated vs. implied
screens.html:
Information in a text comes in two forms.

Stated (explicit)Implied (implicit)
What it meansThe text says it in so many words.The text gives clues and leaves the conclusion to you.
Example“Dana was angry.”“Dana slammed the door so hard that the pictures shook.”
Question wordsAccording to the passage…It can be inferred… The author suggests… most likely…

Both Dana sentences tell you she is angry, but only the first one says the word. When a question says “according to the passage,” the answer is stated; go find it. When a question says “infer” or “suggest,” the answer is not written anywhere. You have to build it from clues.

check.prompt: Which sentence states directly that Luis is tired?
check.hint: Look for the sentence that names how Luis feels, instead of showing an action.
check.explain: Only the first sentence uses a word that names his condition: “exhausted.” The other three show actions (eyes closing, extra coffee, sleeping through alarms) that let you infer he is tired. They imply it; they do not state it.
options: Luis was exhausted after working a double shift.
Luis's eyes kept closing during the bus ride home.
Luis poured his third cup of coffee before noon.
Luis set two alarms and slept through both of them.
why: Closing eyes is a clue that Luis is tired, but the sentence never says so. That makes his tiredness implied, not stated.
Three cups of coffee might suggest he is tired, but the sentence never says it. You inferred the tiredness from his action.
Sleeping through alarms hints that he is worn out, but the word for his condition never appears. It is implied.

screens.title: Imply or infer?
screens.html:
These two words are partners, and the GED uses both.

The writer or speaker implies: hints at an idea without saying it.

The reader or listener infers: figures out the idea from the hints.

Think of it as a ball being thrown and caught. The writer throws the hint (implies). The reader catches it (infers). A question that asks “What does the author imply?” and a question that asks “What can the reader infer?” are asking you to do the same work from two directions.

You will also see suggest, which means the same thing as imply: “The author suggests that the plan will fail.”

check.prompt:
Type one word to complete the sentence.

In her memo, the manager never uses the word “layoffs,” but she ______ that layoffs are coming.
check.hint: Is the manager sending the hint or figuring it out?
check.explain: The manager is the writer. She hints at layoffs without naming them, so she implies (or suggests) that layoffs are coming. The people who read her memo infer it.

mistakes.why: The manager is the writer, so she does not infer. Writers imply (send the hint); readers infer (catch it).
The sentence says she never uses the word “layoffs,” so she does not state it. She hints at it: she implies it.

screens.title: The inference formula
screens.html:
Every good inference is built the same way:

Text clues + what you already know = inference

The clues must come from the text. What you already know is only the glue that connects them. It never replaces them. A helpful organizer has three columns:

Text clueWhat I knowSo I can infer
A man comes in with a dripping umbrella and wet shoes.Rain makes things wet.It is raining outside.

An inference is not a wild guess. It is the conclusion the clues lead a careful reader to, and you can always point to the words that got you there.

example.prompt: “The cashier glanced at the long line, then at the clock, and opened a second register without being asked.” What can you infer about the cashier?
steps: Clues: she notices the long line and the time, and she opens a register on her own.
What I know: opening another register shortens a line; doing it unasked shows initiative.
Inference: she wants to keep customers from waiting and takes action without being told.
example.answer: The cashier is attentive and takes initiative to help customers move faster.

check.prompt:
“Ms. Greer came into the office shaking water from her coat and said the parking lot had turned into a lake.”

What can you infer?
check.hint: What two clues involve water? What usually causes both?
check.explain: Clues: she is shaking water from her coat, and the parking lot is so full of water she calls it a lake. What you know: people get wet and lots flood in heavy rain. Inference: it is raining hard. The drainage choice is tempting because it sounds like a real explanation, but no words in the text point to it.
options: It is raining heavily outside.
The parking lot floods because of poor drainage.
Ms. Greer arrived late for work that morning.
The office parking lot sits beside a lake.
why: This may be true of many lots in real life, but the text gives no reason for the water. Blaming drainage uses outside knowledge, not text clues.
Nothing in the sentence mentions the time or says she was late. That is a guess with no clue behind it.
You read “turned into a lake” literally. It is an exaggeration: the lot is full of water, not next to a real lake.

screens.title: Four steps and the prove-it test
screens.html:
Use these steps on every inference question:

  1. Read the question. Note who or what it asks about.
  2. Go back to the text. Find that part and mark the clues.
  3. Make your own inference first, in one sentence, before you read the choices.
  4. Prove it. Pick the choice that matches, and point to the words that support it.

Prove-it test: “Where does it say that, or which clues lead there?” If you cannot point to words, the choice is out, no matter how reasonable it sounds.

example.prompt: A sign on a café door reads: “Starting Monday, we will close at 3 p.m. instead of 8 p.m. We are sorry for the inconvenience. We are hiring! Ask at the counter.” What can you infer?
steps: Clues: the café is cutting hours, and the same sign says it is hiring.
Connect: a business that needs workers and is closing early probably does not have enough staff to stay open late.
Check a trap: “The café is going out of business” fails the prove-it test. A business that is hiring is not closing.
example.answer: The café is shortening its hours because it does not have enough workers.

check.prompt: The reader can infer that customers cannot get quarters at the laundromat right now. Click the sentence that best supports this inference.
check.hint: Where would a customer normally get quarters at a laundromat?
check.explain: The inference is about getting quarters at the laundromat. A change machine is where customers would get them, and it is out of order until Thursday. That sentence proves the inference. The “bring quarters” sentence is a strong hint, but it would make sense even if the change machine worked; it is the broken machine that explains the problem.
spans: Welcome to Suds & Spin Laundry.
Machines 4 through 9 accept cards only.
Please bring quarters for machines 1 through 3.
The change machine is out of order until Thursday.
We are sorry for any trouble this causes.
check.why: The most common wrong click is “Please bring quarters for machines 1 through 3.” It tells you that some machines need quarters, but not that the laundromat cannot supply them. Only the broken change machine explains why customers cannot get quarters there.

screens.title: Inference or guess?
screens.html:
Every statement about a text falls into one of three groups:

  • Stated directly: the text says it in so many words.
  • Reasonable inference: the text does not say it, but the clues clearly lead there.
  • Not supported: it might be true, but nothing in the text proves it. It is a guess.

The third group is where wrong answers live. A choice can sound sensible, match what usually happens in real life, and still be unsupported. Before you call something an inference, name the clues that lead to it. If you cannot name any, it is a guess.

“It could be true” is not the same as “the text supports it.”

check.prompt:
“Ms. Patel closed her laptop, put on her coat, and turned off the office lights at 9:40 p.m. On her desk sat a finished grant proposal with a sticky note: ‘Due tomorrow, 8 a.m.’”

Drag each statement into the correct category.
check.hint: For each statement, ask: Are these exact words in the text? If not, do clues lead there? If not, it is not supported.
check.explain: Stated: the 9:40 p.m. lights and the “Due tomorrow, 8 a.m.” note are written out. Inference: nothing says why she stayed, but a finished proposal due the next morning and a 9:40 p.m. departure point clearly to staying late to finish it. Not supported: no boss is mentioned, and nothing tells you how the proposal will be judged.
choices: Ms. Patel turned off the office lights at 9:40 p.m.
Ms. Patel stayed late to finish the grant proposal.
The grant proposal is due the next morning.
Ms. Patel's boss ordered her to stay late.
The proposal will win the grant.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting “Ms. Patel's boss ordered her to stay late” under inference. Staying late does suggest a deadline, but no boss appears in the text, so that statement is a guess.

screens.title: Choosing the best evidence
screens.html:
Many GED questions ask, “Which detail best supports the idea that…?” Several choices will be on the right subject. The best evidence passes three checks:

  • Relevant: it is about the exact idea, not just the same subject.
  • Specific: it gives a fact, number, action, or quotation.
  • Direct: if the detail is true, the idea must be true, or very nearly so.

The key test question is: “If this detail is true, does the idea have to be true?” Weak evidence only makes an idea possible. Strong evidence makes it hard to deny.

example.prompt: Claim: “The town's free tax-help clinic is meeting a real need.” Which detail best supports it? (a) The clinic meets in the library basement. (b) Tax forms have grown more complicated. (c) Volunteers helped 412 residents file this year, and 90 more were still on the waiting list when the season ended.
steps: (a) is about the clinic but says nothing about need.
(b) is general; it does not mention this town and only makes a need possible.
(c) is relevant (demand), specific (412 and 90), and direct (more people wanted help than the clinic could serve).

check.prompt:
Claim: “The city's new evening bus route is popular with riders.”

Which detail best supports this claim?
check.hint: Which detail actually measures how many people use the route?
check.explain: Popularity means many people use something. Only the ridership number measures that: 2,300 riders, twice the forecast. It is relevant, specific, and direct. The evening-shift choice is the most tempting, because it explains why the route could be popular, but it does not show that it is.
options: In its first month, the route carried 2,300 riders, twice the planners' forecast.
The route runs every half hour from 6 p.m. until midnight, seven days a week.
Many people in the city work evening shifts at hospitals, stores, and warehouses.
The new buses on the route are painted green and have room for 40 riders.
why: This describes the schedule, not how many people use it. A route can run every half hour and still be nearly empty.
This is general and only makes popularity possible. It does not show that anyone actually rides this route.
The color and size of the buses say nothing about whether riders use the route. This is true but irrelevant.

screens.title: Relevant, or only on topic?
screens.html:
The hardest wrong answers on evidence questions are details that are on the topic but do not prove the claim. If the claim is “The pantry cannot keep up with demand,” a detail about who runs the pantry is on the topic (the pantry) but says nothing about demand.

To sort them, underline the key words in the claim. Here they are cannot keep up and demand. Then ask of each detail: does it show that more people need help than the pantry can serve? Details about history, location, staff, or general trends usually fail, even when they are true.

When a question says “Select two,” test each choice on its own against the claim. Two choices may support it in different ways.

check.prompt:
Claim: “The Riverside food pantry cannot keep up with demand.”

Which two details best support the claim? Select two answers.
check.hint: Underline “cannot keep up.” Which details show more need than the pantry can meet?
check.explain: The claim has two key ideas: demand and falling short. Running out of fresh food by 11 a.m. shows the supply runs out before the need does. A waiting list of 85 families shows people who need help and are not getting it yet. The food-price detail is the most tempting, but it is about the region, not about this pantry.
options: Last month, the pantry ran out of fresh food by 11 a.m. on three of its four open days.
The pantry keeps a waiting list of 85 families for its weekly grocery boxes.
The pantry is run by volunteers from four local churches and a high school club.
Food prices in the region have risen about 9 percent over the past year.
The pantry moved to a larger building on Pine Street in 2019.
why: This tells who runs the pantry. It is on the topic but says nothing about whether the pantry can meet demand.
This is a general trend. Rising prices might increase need, but this detail does not show anything about this pantry's supply.
A move to a larger building is about the pantry's history. If anything, it suggests the pantry grew; it does not show it is falling short now.

screens.title: Paired questions
screens.html:
The GED often links two questions:

  • Part A asks for an inference: “What can be inferred about…?”
  • Part B asks for the proof: “Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?”

Work them together. When you answer Part A, put your cursor on the line that led you there. That line is usually the answer to Part B. If your Part B evidence does not prove your Part A answer, one of them is wrong; go back and check both.

Watch for Part B choices that support a different Part A choice. Test makers include evidence for the tempting wrong inference, hoping you will match the two mistakes.

check.prompt:
“Dominic had worked at the warehouse for six years. When the night-shift supervisor job opened, he stayed after his shift every evening for two weeks to study the safety manual. His interview was on a Monday morning. Afterward, he told his sister, ‘I don't want to jinx it.’”

Part A answer: Dominic wants the supervisor job badly enough to give up his own time for it.

Part B. Which detail best supports that answer?
check.hint: The claim says he gives up his own time. Which detail shows him doing that?
check.explain: The Part A answer has two parts: he wants the job, and he gives up his own time for it. Staying after his shift every evening for two weeks proves both. The “jinx” line is the most tempting, because it shows he cares, but it does not prove the second part of the claim.
options: He stayed after his shift every evening for two weeks to study the manual.
He had worked at the warehouse for six years before the supervisor job opened.
His interview for the supervisor job took place on a Monday morning.
He told his sister after the interview, “I don't want to jinx it.”
why: Six years shows experience, not desire. It does not show him giving up any of his own time.
The day of the interview is true but irrelevant. It says nothing about how much he wants the job.
This shows he hopes he gets the job, but it does not show him giving up his own time, which is the exact claim.

screens.title: Inferences about characters
screens.html:
Fiction writers rarely name a character's feelings. They show them. Look for four kinds of clues:

Sayswords, tone, short answers, what is left unsaid
Doesactions, gestures, body language
Thinksthoughts the narrator shares
Others reacthow other characters treat them

Actions often speak louder than words. A character who says “I'm fine” while gripping the steering wheel is not fine. Put the clues together, just as you would with an informational text, and state the feeling or motive in a few words. Then make sure you can point to the clues.

check.prompt:
“Grandpa Lou read the letter from the bank, folded it into a small square, and put it in his shirt pocket. When his daughter asked what it said, he picked up the remote and turned the TV volume up.”

What can you infer?
check.hint: What does he do with the letter, and what does he do when asked about it?
check.explain: Does: he folds the letter small and pockets it (hides it). Reaction to a question: he turns the TV up instead of answering (avoids it). Together these show the letter holds news he does not want to discuss. The account choice is tempting because bank letters can bring bad news, but naming the exact news goes beyond the clues.
options: The letter has news that Lou does not want to talk about.
Lou did not hear his daughter's question over the loud TV.
The bank has closed Lou's account and kept his savings.
Lou is excited to show his daughter the letter later.
why: He turns the volume up after she asks, so the TV was not drowning her out. Turning it up is a way to avoid answering.
This is overreach. The clues show the letter is unwelcome, but nothing tells you what it says.
This is contradicted. Hiding the letter in his pocket and avoiding the question show the opposite of eagerness to share.

screens.title: When characters don't say what they mean
screens.html:
People in stories, like people in life, often say one thing and mean another. Watch for:

  • Sarcasm: saying the opposite of what you mean (“Oh, great” after bad news).
  • Dry humor: a mild joke about something serious.
  • Exaggeration: “I've told you a million times.”
  • Short or missing answers: a silence or a one-word reply can show hurt or anger.

To find the real meaning, read what happens just before the line. The situation tells you the tone.

example.prompt: “Mr. Ortiz looked at the dented fender, then at his teenage son, then back at the fender. ‘Well,’ he said, ‘I guess you found the mailbox.’” What does he mean?
steps: Situation: a dented fender, and his son is the one he looks at.
The line: “found the mailbox” is a mild way to say the son hit it.
Meaning: he knows his son hit a mailbox with the car and is making a dry joke about it. It does not mean he does not care.
example.answer: The son hit a mailbox, and Mr. Ortiz is responding with dry humor.

check.prompt:
“After the third customer in a row complained about the slow line, Bree turned to her coworker and said, ‘I just love Mondays.’”

What does Bree most likely mean?
check.hint: Read what just happened. Would someone really mean that after three complaints?
check.explain: Read what happens just before the line: three complaints in a row about a slow line. In that situation, “I just love Mondays” is sarcasm. Bree means the day is going badly and she is frustrated. The literal reading is the main trap.
options: She is frustrated with how the workday is going.
Monday is her favorite day of the week to work.
She wants her manager to move her to another day.
She enjoys handling complaints from customers.
why: You took the line literally. Right after three complaints, “I just love Mondays” is sarcasm: she means the opposite.
This is overreach. She is venting about today; nothing shows she wants a schedule change.
This is contradicted by the situation. Three complaints in a row are not something people enjoy; the line is sarcastic.

screens.title: Tracking a character's change
screens.html:
Many story questions ask how a character feels at one moment, or how the character changes. Feelings in a story are rarely fixed. A character can start nervous and end confident, or start hopeful and end let down.

To track a change, mark the clues in order. Ask, “How does the character act at the start? What do they do differently by the end? What happened in between?” The shift in actions is your evidence.

When a question names a paragraph or moment, answer for that moment only. A character's feeling at the end of a story is not the answer to a question about the beginning.

check.prompt:
(1) Theo arrived at the job fair twenty minutes before the doors opened. (2) He had printed ten copies of his résumé. (3) At the first table, he shook the recruiter's hand and then wiped his palm on his pants. (4) He forgot the name of his last employer for a moment. (5) By the third table, he was laughing and trading stories with the recruiters.

Which sentence shows that Theo had become more comfortable? Type the sentence number.
check.hint: Look for a time phrase that signals a change, and an action that shows ease.
check.explain: Sentences 3 and 4 show nerves: a sweaty palm and a memory slip. Sentence 5 shows a change: “By the third table,” he was laughing and trading stories. People laugh and chat easily when they feel comfortable. Answer: 5.

mistakes.why: Wiping a sweaty palm shows Theo was nervous at the start. The question asks for the moment he became more comfortable.
Forgetting his last employer's name shows nerves, not comfort. Look for the sentence where his behavior changes.
Arriving early and printing résumés show that Theo prepared and cared, but not that he felt at ease. Find the sentence that shows a change.

screens.title: The four inference traps
screens.html:
Wrong answers on inference questions are not random. Most fall into one of four traps:

TrapWhat it looks likeAsk yourself
OverreachGoes further than the clues; often uses all, never, always, onlyDo the clues really go this far?
Outside knowledgeMight be true in real life, but the text does not support itCould I reach this from the text alone?
ContradictedThe text says or shows the oppositeDoes any line say otherwise?
True but irrelevantA real detail from the text that does not answer the questionDoes this answer what was asked?

Name the trap every time you cross out a choice. It makes your eliminations faster and more confident.

check.prompt:
“In the two years since Oak Avenue got protected bike lanes, crashes on the street fell by 40 percent. Some shop owners worried about losing parking, but sales on the avenue have held steady.”

Question: What can be inferred about the bike lanes on Oak Avenue? Name the trap in each wrong answer.

“The bike lanes are the only reason crashes on Oak Avenue went down.” {{0}}

“The bike lanes have hurt sales at Oak Avenue shops.” {{1}}

“Biking to work is the healthiest way to commute.” {{2}}
check.hint: Compare each choice with the text: Does it go too far, say the opposite, or bring in something the text never mentions?
check.explain: Choice 1 is overreach: the text links the lanes to a 40 percent drop in crashes, but it never says the lanes were the only reason. The extreme word “only” stretches a true clue too far. Choice 2 is contradicted: the text says sales held steady. Choice 3 is outside knowledge: it may be true, but the paragraph says nothing about health.

options: overreach
outside knowledge
contradicted
true but irrelevant
why: This starts from a real clue in the text, the drop in crashes after the lanes went in, and stretches it with the extreme word “only.” Stretching a true clue too far is overreach; outside knowledge brings in facts the text never mentions.
The text never names any other cause, so it does not say the opposite. It simply does not go as far as “the only reason.”
This is not a detail the text states. The text says crashes fell after the lanes went in; it never says the lanes were the only cause.

options: overreach
outside knowledge
contradicted
true but irrelevant
why: Overreach stretches something true. This choice says the opposite of the text: sales held steady.
This is not borrowed from real life. The text speaks to sales directly and says they held steady, so the choice is contradicted.
This is not a true detail. The text says sales held steady, which is the opposite of “hurt sales.”

options: overreach
outside knowledge
contradicted
true but irrelevant
why: Overreach stretches a clue from the text too far. The text has no clue about health at all; this comes from outside it.
The text never discusses health, so it does not say the opposite. It simply does not support this idea.
This is not a detail from the text at all. A true-but-irrelevant choice repeats something the text actually says.

screens.title: Overreach and extreme words
screens.html:
Overreach is the most common trap on inference questions. The choice starts from something true in the text and then pushes it too far. Watch for:

  • extreme words: all, every, never, always, only, completely, proves
  • a jump from some to most, or from one time to a pattern
  • a reason or cause the text never gives

A safe inference often sounds a little modest: some, many, may, helped. But do not treat extreme words as automatically wrong. If the text says “every seat was filled,” a choice that says “every” can be right. Always check against the words in the text.

check.prompt:
“Since the factory opened a free on-site day care center, the share of new parents who return to work after their leave has risen from 61 percent to 83 percent.”

Which inference is best supported?
check.hint: Compare 83 percent with “every.” Which choice stays within the numbers?
check.explain: The return rate rose from 61 to 83 percent after the day care center opened, so it is reasonable to infer the center helped some parents return. “Every” is overreach: 83 percent leaves 17 percent who did not return.
options: Every new parent at the factory now returns to work after leave.
The day care center has made it easier for some parents to return.
The factory pays higher wages than other employers in the area.
Fewer new parents return to the factory now than before it opened.
why: This is overreach. 83 percent is a large share, but it is not every parent; 17 percent still do not return.
This is outside knowledge. Pay is never mentioned; the only change described is the day care center.
This is contradicted. The share went up, from 61 to 83 percent, not down.

screens.title: What does the line most likely mean?
screens.html:
Some questions ask what a speaker or writer “most likely means” by a line. The line is usually not meant literally. It might be a figure of speech, a joke, an exaggeration, or a hint at something the speaker does not want to say outright.

  1. Read the sentences just before and just after the line.
  2. Ask what the situation is and how the speaker feels.
  3. Restate the line in plain words that fit that situation.

The trap answer is usually the literal meaning, or a meaning that fits the words but ignores what happens next.

check.prompt:
“When the moving truck finally pulled away with the last of her son's things, Mrs. Lin looked around the empty living room. ‘Well,’ she said, ‘the house is quiet enough now.’ Then she climbed the stairs and sat for a long time on her son's bare mattress.”

What does Mrs. Lin most likely mean?
check.hint: Read what she does right after she speaks. What does that action show?
check.explain: Read past the line. After saying the house is “quiet enough now,” she sits for a long time on her son's bare mattress. The quiet is the quiet of her son being gone, and her action shows she misses him. The movers choice is the main trap: it fits the words but ignores what she does next.
options: She is glad the noisy movers have finally gone.
She plans to sell the house now that it is empty.
She misses her son, and the quiet makes his absence real.
She is angry that her son left without a goodbye.
why: The line alone could mean this, but the next sentence shows her sitting a long time on her son's bare mattress. That is sadness, not relief.
Nothing in the passage mentions selling the house. This goes beyond the clues.
Nothing suggests he left without a goodbye or that she is angry. Sitting quietly on his mattress shows loss, not anger.

screens.title: Why did the author include that?
screens.html:
Another common inference question asks why an author included a detail, a quotation, or a paragraph. The answer is about the detail's job, not just what it says. Common jobs:

  • to give proof for a claim
  • to show a contrast that makes something else stand out
  • to set up a problem that the next part solves
  • to raise a worry or objection that the evidence then answers

Look at what comes right before and after the detail, and watch for signal words such as however, instead, and that is exactly why.

example.prompt: “(1) A council member argued that most people would never return the tools they borrowed. (2) Last year the tool library made 4,850 loans. (3) Only 4 tools never came back.” Why does the author include sentence 1?
steps: Sentence 1 states a worry: people will not return tools.
Sentences 2 and 3 give the result: thousands of loans, almost no losses.
So sentence 1's job is to set up a doubt that the evidence then shows was wrong.
example.answer: To raise an early worry that the numbers then answer.

check.prompt:
“(1) Some parents feared that a later school start time would only mean students stayed up later. (2) At Ridgeway High, which moved its first bell from 7:20 to 8:30, a survey found that students slept an average of 34 more minutes per night. (3) Late arrivals fell by a third.”

Why does the author most likely include sentence 1?
check.hint: What does sentence 2 show about the fear in sentence 1?
check.explain: Sentence 1 states a fear: students would just stay up later. Sentence 2 answers it: students actually slept 34 more minutes. So sentence 1's job is to raise a concern that the evidence then shows was wrong. The “most parents” choice is tempting, but “some” is not “most,” and the question asks about the sentence's job.
options: to argue that parents should set earlier bedtimes for teenagers
to show that most parents were against the change at Ridgeway
to raise a concern that the survey results then answer
to explain how the Ridgeway sleep survey was carried out
why: The passage never tells parents what to do about bedtimes. This invents an argument the text does not make.
This is overreach. Sentence 1 says “some parents,” not most, and its job is to set up the results.
Sentence 1 says nothing about how the survey worked. It states a fear, which sentence 2 then tests.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • Information can be stated (explicit) or implied (implicit). The writer implies; the reader infers.
  • Text clues + what you already know = inference. The clues must come from the text.
  • Use the four steps: read the question, go back to the text, make your own inference first, then prove it by pointing to the words.
  • The best evidence is relevant, specific, and direct: if it is true, the idea must be true.
  • On paired questions, the line that led you to Part A is usually the answer to Part B.
  • In fiction, infer from what characters say, do, and think, and how others react. Read the situation to catch sarcasm, jokes, and exaggeration.
  • For “most likely means” and “why include” questions, read the sentences just before and after.
  • Name the trap on every wrong answer: overreach, outside knowledge, contradicted, true but irrelevant.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: The Day the Ice Goes Out
stimuli.html:
[1] For more than 140 years, someone in Calder Lake has waited each spring for “ice-out”: the day a boat could cross from the town dock to Gull Island without touching ice. A ferry operator named Amos Whitlock began recording the date in his logbook in 1882. He had a practical reason. Until the ice went out, his ferry could not run.

[2] Whitlock's logbook now sits in a glass case at the town historical society, and the tradition he started has never stopped. The job passed to the town's postmaster, then to a science teacher, and since 1998 to a team of volunteers. The rule for declaring ice-out has never changed.

[3] For over a century, the record was local trivia, and residents placed small bets on the date. Then, in the early 2000s, Dr. Nadia Ferro, a university scientist, came across the logbook. “I was looking at one of the longest unbroken climate records in the region,” she said, “kept by people who had no idea that was what they were doing.”

[4] Ferro compared the dates by decade. In the 1880s, the ice went out, on average, on April 29. In the 2010s, the average was April 14. The change has not been steady; some recent springs have been late. But the overall direction is clear. Ferro notes that a single year tells you about weather, while a long record tells you about climate. “Any one date can fool you,” she said. “A hundred and forty dates are much harder to argue with.”

[5] The thaw also affects when tiny organisms bloom in the lake, which affects what young fish such as lake trout eat. Ray Ostrowski, who owns a bait shop by the dock, says ice fishing season, which once lasted well into March, now often ends weeks earlier. “Ten years ago, people were still buying ice augers from me in the middle of March,” he said. “Now I put them in storage by the end of February.”

[6] Ferro's team has since found eleven similar records elsewhere, including a church diary that noted when a river froze each winter and a mill owner's notes on when his millpond thawed. Not every record is usable. Some have gaps of many years, and some writers changed their rules for what counted as “frozen.” Ferro says that is exactly why the Calder Lake record is so valuable. “The same question, asked the same way, at the same spot, for 140 years,” she said.

[7] The volunteers say the attention has not changed how they do the job. They still walk to the dock each morning with a notebook, and they still declare ice-out only when a boat could reach Gull Island without touching ice. One of them, a retired nurse named Ellen Pryce, keeps a yellowed newspaper clipping on her refrigerator. It reports that she won the town bet in 1987 with a guess of April 20. “I'd never win with that guess now,” she said, laughing.

stimuli.title: The Key Ring
stimuli.html:
An original short story.

[1] The bus let Teresa off a block early, so she walked the rest of the way past the laundromat and the empty shoe store, practicing under her breath. Good morning, Mr. Haddad. Thank you for this opportunity. I am a hard worker and a fast learner. She had repeated the words so many times on the ride that they had stopped sounding like words at all.

[2] Haddad Hardware smelled of sawdust and machine oil. Behind the counter, a gray-haired man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead was sorting bolts into a metal tray. He did not look up when the bell over the door rang.

[3] “You're the one Delia sent,” he said.

[4] “Yes, sir. Teresa Lowe. Thank you for this—”

[5] “Can you cut a key?”

[6] She looked at the machine at the end of the counter, a squat gray box with two clamps and a grinding wheel. Her uncle had kept one exactly like it in the back of his garage, where she had spent most of the summer she turned twelve. “I haven't done it in a while,” she said.

[7] He slid a brass key across the counter without a word, then took a blank from a hook on the wall and set it beside the first. Teresa fastened both in the clamps, checked that their edges lined up, and tightened the knobs. Her hands seemed to remember before she did. The wheel whined, and a fine brass dust settled on her sleeve. When she was done, she ran her thumb along the new key's teeth, the way her uncle had shown her, found one rough spot, and smoothed it with a file before she handed the key back.

[8] Mr. Haddad held the two keys up to the window, side by side. He turned them over and held them up again. Then he put the old key in a drawer and dropped the new one into his own shirt pocket.

[9] He reached under the counter, brought out a ring holding four keys, and set it in front of her.

[10] “Front door, back door, register, storeroom,” he said. “I come in at seven. You open on Saturdays.” He went back to his bolts. “The coffee maker's broken. Fix that and you can stay forever.”

[11] Teresa closed her hand around the ring. It was heavier than it looked. She thought of the speech she had practiced on the bus and understood that she would never need to give it. Outside, a bus rumbled past the window, and for the first time in months, she did not check the time to see when the next one would come.

stimuli.title: Draft Notice: Boiler Replacement
stimuli.html:
To: All Residents of Linden Court Apartments
From: Building Management
Date: September 21
Subject: Boiler replacement on Tuesday, October 6

(1) Last January, our building's boiler broke down twice, and residents went without heat for a combined total of three days. After the second breakdown, the repair company told us that the boiler, which is 31 years old, could no longer be fixed reliably because (A) replacement parts are no longer made. (B) we have arranged to replace it before the cold weather returns.

(2) On Tuesday, October 6, the heat and hot water will be shut off from 8:00 a.m. to about 6:00 p.m. while the crew removes the old boiler and connects the new one. The laundry room will also be closed that day, because the washing machines use the building's hot water. Workers will need to reach the back wall of the basement storage area, so please move any items stored against the back wall of your storage unit by Monday evening, October 5.

(3) We understand that a day without hot water is an inconvenience. Any resident who has a medical need for hot water on October 6 should contact the office by Friday, October 2, so that we can make other arrangements. The community room on the first floor will stay open all day, and coffee and snacks will be provided.

(4) The new boiler is designed to use about 25 percent less gas than the old one. The savings from the new boiler's lower gas use (C) expected to help keep future rent increases small. Thank you for your patience as we make this improvement.

stimuli.title: The Tool Library on Fenwick Street
stimuli.html:
[1] When Grace Okafor bought her first house in 2014, she discovered that the gutters needed cleaning, the porch steps were loose, and she owned exactly one hammer. A ladder, a drill, and a set of clamps would have cost her more than $400. “I was going to use each of them maybe twice a year,” she said. Instead, she pinned a note to the bulletin board at the corner laundromat asking whether a neighbor would lend her a ladder for an afternoon. By the end of the week, six people had called.

[2] Two of the callers asked whether they could borrow something from her in return. That gave Okafor an idea. In the spring of 2015, she and four neighbors set up shelves in her garage and stocked them with 60 donated tools. Anyone who lived in the city could borrow a tool for a week at no charge. The only rule, written in marker on the garage door, was “Bring it back cleaner than you found it.”

[3] The Fenwick Street Tool Library now fills a former bakery and lends more than 1,100 tools, from pressure washers to tile saws. Last year it recorded 4,850 loans, up from about 300 in its first year. It still charges nothing, though a jar by the door collects donations.

[4] The library has also collected information its founders never expected. Volunteers log every loan by hand in a binder, and in 2021 city planners noticed a pattern: loans of dehumidifiers and wet-dry vacuums jumped every time the river rose, and the borrowers' addresses clustered on the same six blocks. “Those binders showed us exactly which streets flood, even in storms too small to make the news,” said Paul Medina, a city engineer. The city has since budgeted for new storm drains on four of those blocks.

[5] Not everyone was convinced at first. When Okafor applied for a city grant in 2017, one council member argued that most borrowers would never return the tools. The library's records answer that worry. Of last year's 4,850 loans, 31 tools came back late and 4 never came back at all. “People treat the tools like they belong to a neighbor,” Okafor said, “because they do.”

[6] Hardware store owner Dale Kessler admits he was worried when the library opened two blocks from his shop. “I figured nobody would buy a drill again,” he said. Instead, he says, his sales of screws, paint, lumber, and other supplies have grown, and he now donates a tool to the library every month. “Somebody who borrows a tile saw still has to buy the tile,” he said.

[7] Other towns have called to ask how to start their own libraries. Okafor tells them that the tools are the easy part. “Anybody can collect a shelf of drills,” she said. “What you're really building is the habit of asking your neighbors for help.”

stimuli.title: Pencil and Marker
stimuli.html:
An original short story.

[1] Andre got to Ruiz Bakery at 3:50 a.m., ten minutes early, and stood under the dark awning with his hands in his jacket pockets. He had set three alarms the night before. He had not needed any of them.

[2] Mrs. Ruiz unlocked the door at four exactly. She was a short woman with flour already on her forearms, and she looked at his clean white sneakers for a long moment before she stepped aside to let him in.

[3] “My nephew says you can bake,” she said.

[4] “Yes, ma'am. I mean, I've made bread at home, mostly. I watched a lot of videos and—”

[5] “Conchas,” she said, and pointed to a bowl of dough rising under a towel. “Two trays. The topping is in the green tub.”

[6] His first tray came out pale on top and dark on the bottom. He stared at it and felt the heat climb up his neck. Mrs. Ruiz did not say anything. She reached past him, turned the oven dial a quarter turn, moved the rack up one notch, and went back to her own work. He shaped the second tray more slowly, pressing the striped topping onto each roll the way he had seen her press hers, and this time he watched the oven window instead of the clock.

[7] When the second tray came out, the tops were cracked and golden. Mrs. Ruiz broke one roll in half, smelled it, and ate both halves standing at the counter. Then she wiped her hands on her apron and walked to the schedule taped beside the walk-in cooler. Next to his name, which was written in pencil, was the word TRIAL. She crossed out the word and wrote “Andre” again underneath, in black marker.

[8] “The first tray goes to the church pantry,” she said, already turning away. “Burn another one, and you're eating it for lunch.”

[9] Andre looked down at his sneakers. They were white with flour now, almost to the laces. He did not brush them off.
