items.prompt: Based on paragraph 1, what can the reader infer about why Amos Whitlock recorded the ice-out date?
items.hint: Paragraph 1 says he had “a practical reason.” What could he not do until the ice went out?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the clues. Paragraph 1 says Whitlock was a ferry operator, that he had “a practical reason,” and that “until the ice went out, his ferry could not run.”

Step 2. Connect them with what you know: a ferry operator earns money by running the ferry. If the ferry could not run until ice-out, the date marked when his work, and his income, could begin again.

Step 3. The ferry-income choice matches. Correct. The climate choice is the most tempting because the record later became a climate record, but paragraph 3 says the keepers “had no idea” that was what they were doing.
options: Ice-out told him when his ferry could start earning money again.
He was trying to measure how the region's climate was changing.
The town paid him to keep an official yearly record of the lake.
He wanted to win the bet that residents placed on the date.
why: This is contradicted. Paragraph 3 says the record keepers “had no idea” they were keeping a climate record; that use came more than a century later.
This is not supported. The passage never mentions pay. Paragraph 1 gives a different “practical reason”: his ferry could not run until ice-out.
This is not supported. The bets appear in paragraph 3 and are never connected to Whitlock; paragraph 1 ties his reason to his ferry.

items.prompt: The reader can infer that ice-out on Calder Lake now usually comes earlier than it did in 1987. Click the sentence from paragraph 7 that best supports this inference.
items.hint: One sentence tells you what happened in 1987. Which sentence tells you how things are different now?
items.explain:
Step 1. The inference compares two times: 1987 and now. The best evidence must say something about the present.

Step 2. The sentence before it tells us that a guess of April 20 won in 1987, so the ice went out around April 20 that year.

Step 3. Pryce says, “I'd never win with that guess now.” If April 20 would not win today, ice-out now comes on a different date, and paragraph 4 shows the trend is toward earlier dates (an average of April 14 in the 2010s). Correct. The first two sentences describe the volunteers' routine, which is true but irrelevant.
spans: The volunteers say the attention has not changed how they do the job.
They still walk to the dock each morning with a notebook, and they still declare ice-out only when a boat could reach Gull Island without touching ice.
One of them, a retired nurse named Ellen Pryce, keeps a yellowed newspaper clipping on her refrigerator.
It reports that she won the town bet in 1987 with a guess of April 20.
“I'd never win with that guess now,” she said, laughing.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the 1987 bet. It gives the old date, but on its own it says nothing about today, so it cannot show a change. Pryce's remark about “now” is what compares then with today.

items.prompt: Based on Ray Ostrowski's statements in paragraph 5, what can the reader infer?
items.hint: Ice fishing needs ice. Why would the season end earlier?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the clues. Ice fishing season “once lasted well into March” and “now often ends weeks earlier.” Ostrowski used to sell ice augers (tools for drilling through ice) in mid-March but now stores them by the end of February.

Step 2. Connect them: ice fishing can happen only when the ice is solid. If the season ends weeks earlier, the ice is no longer solid as late into the year.

Step 3. The shorter-time choice matches, and it fits the passage's central point that the lake thaws earlier. Correct. The interest choice is the main trap: fewer augers sold might seem to mean less interest, but Ostrowski ties the change to the season ending, not to customers losing interest.
options: The lake now stays frozen enough for ice fishing for a shorter time.
Fewer people in Calder Lake are interested in ice fishing these days.
Lake trout have disappeared from Calder Lake in the past ten years.
Ostrowski plans to stop selling ice fishing equipment at his shop.
why: This is not supported. Paragraph 5 says the season ends earlier, which depends on the ice. It says nothing about how many people want to fish.
This is overreach. Paragraph 5 says only that the thaw affects what young fish such as lake trout eat; it never says the trout are gone.
This is not supported. Ostrowski puts the augers in storage, which suggests he will bring them out and sell them again.

items.prompt: Dr. Ferro believes the Calder Lake record is especially valuable for studying climate. Which two details from the passage best support her view? Select two answers.
items.hint: Reread Ferro's quotation at the end of paragraph 6. What two qualities does she praise?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find Ferro's reasons. In paragraph 3 she calls it “one of the longest unbroken climate records.” In paragraph 6 she explains its value: “The same question, asked the same way, at the same spot, for 140 years.”

Step 2. Those words point to two qualities: the method never changed, and the record is long and unbroken.

Step 3. The unchanged rule (paragraph 2) shows the same method. The unbroken 140-year span (paragraphs 1–3) shows length with no gaps. Both correct. The church diary is the most tempting wrong choice because it is also a record, but it is not the Calder Lake record.
options: The rule for declaring ice-out has stayed the same since the record began.
The record has continued without a break for more than 140 years.
Residents placed small bets on the ice-out date each year.
Whitlock's logbook is displayed in a glass case at the historical society.
Some recent springs have had late ice-out dates.
A church diary recorded when a river froze each winter.
why: The bets are true but irrelevant. They made the date a local game; they do not make the data more useful for science.
Where the logbook is kept says nothing about the quality of the record. This is true but irrelevant.
Late recent springs complicate the trend; they are not a reason the record is valuable.
This is a different record, and paragraph 6 suggests some of those other records are less reliable.

items.prompt: Use paragraph 4. By how many days did the average ice-out date move between the 1880s and the 2010s? Type the number.
items.hint: Both dates are in April. Subtract the day numbers.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the two averages in paragraph 4: April 29 in the 1880s and April 14 in the 2010s.

Step 2. Both dates are in April, so subtract the day numbers: 29 − 14 = 15.

Answer: 15 days earlier. This number is the evidence behind the passage's central inference: ice-out now comes earlier than it used to.

mistakes.why: You counted both April 29 and April 14 as days. The change from April 29 to April 14 is 29 − 14 = 15 days.
That is one of the dates, not the change. Subtract the two average dates: April 29 − April 14 = 15 days.
140 is the number of years the record covers, not the change in the ice-out date. Use the two averages in paragraph 4.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, Dr. Ferro says, “Any one date can fool you.” What does she most likely mean?
items.hint: Read the sentences just before the quotation. What is the difference between weather and climate?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the context. Just before the quotation, the passage says the change has not been steady (some recent springs were late) and that “a single year tells you about weather, while a long record tells you about climate.”

Step 2. Ferro follows with, “A hundred and forty dates are much harder to argue with.” She is contrasting one date with many.

Step 3. So “fool you” means one unusual year could mislead you about the long-term pattern. Correct. The wrong-date choice is tempting if you read “fool” literally.
options: A single early or late spring could give a false picture of the trend.
The volunteers have sometimes recorded the wrong ice-out date.
Ice-out dates have no real connection to changes in climate.
The dates recorded in the 1880s are less accurate than recent ones.
why: This takes “fool” too literally. Nothing in the passage suggests mistakes in the record; Ferro is talking about how to read the dates.
This is contradicted. Ferro says the long record shows a clear direction, so she does think the dates reveal something about climate.
This is not supported. The passage never questions the older dates; Ferro praises the record for being consistent.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 1 and 4, how does Teresa most likely feel as she arrives at Haddad Hardware?
items.hint: What is she doing as she walks, and how many times has she done it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Gather clues from what Teresa does and says. In paragraph 1 she practices a speech “under her breath” and has repeated it “so many times” that the words have lost their meaning. In paragraph 4 she starts her prepared, polite thank-you.

Step 2. Connect them: people rehearse over and over when they are anxious about something that matters to them.

Step 3. “Nervous and eager to make a good impression” fits. Correct. The confident choice is the main trap if you jump ahead to how well she cuts the key later.
options: nervous and eager to make a good impression
confident because she has worked at the store before
irritated that the bus let her off a block early
unsure whether she wants the job at all
why: This is contradicted. Mr. Haddad knows her only as “the one Delia sent,” so they are meeting for the first time, and her rehearsing shows nerves, not confidence.
This is not supported. The story mentions the early stop, but Teresa shows no annoyance; she uses the walk to practice.
This is contradicted by all her preparation. People do not rehearse a speech over and over for a job they do not want.

items.prompt: Mr. Haddad never says, “You're hired.” Which detail from the story best supports the inference that he has decided to hire Teresa?
items.hint: Which action would a boss take only after deciding to trust a new worker?
items.explain:
Step 1. The inference is that he has decided to hire her. The best evidence must show a decision, not a test.

Step 2. Holding the keys to the window is checking; asking “Can you cut a key?” starts the test; not looking up is just his manner.

Step 3. Handing her the keys to the front door, back door, register, and storeroom and saying, “You open on Saturdays,” only makes sense if she now works there. It is relevant, specific, and direct. Correct.
options: He gives her a ring of store keys and says she will open on Saturdays.
He holds the two keys up to the window, side by side, and turns them over.
He slides a brass key across the counter and asks, “Can you cut a key?”
He keeps sorting bolts and does not look up when the bell over the door rings.
why: This shows him checking her work. It comes before any decision, so it does not prove he has decided to hire her.
This starts the test. Asking whether she can cut a key shows he is still deciding, not that he has decided.
This shows his gruff manner when she arrives. It is true but irrelevant to whether he hires her.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category based on the story.
items.hint: For each statement, ask: Does the story say this in so many words? If not, do the clues lead there? If not, it is not supported.
items.explain:
Stated directly: “Her uncle had kept one exactly like it in the back of his garage” (paragraph 6). “I come in at seven” (paragraph 10).

Reasonable inference: The story never says Teresa cut keys before, but she says, “I haven't done it in a while,” she spent a summer in her uncle's garage near the same machine, and “her hands seemed to remember.” The story never says Mr. Haddad is satisfied, but he checks the key twice, puts it in his own pocket, and hands her the store keys.

Not supported: Delia is named only as the person who sent Teresa; nothing says how she is related to Mr. Haddad. Pay is never mentioned.
choices: Teresa's uncle kept a key-cutting machine in his garage.
Mr. Haddad comes in to the store at seven.
Teresa had cut keys before, years earlier.
Mr. Haddad is satisfied with the key Teresa made.
Teresa will earn more than the store's other workers.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting “Teresa had cut keys before” under “Stated directly.” The story never says it in so many words; you infer it from “I haven't done it in a while” and “her hands seemed to remember.” Another common mistake is calling Delia his daughter, which is a guess.

items.prompt:
Read the draft notice. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): …the boiler, which is 31 years old, could no longer be fixed reliably because {{0}} replacement parts are no longer made.

Paragraph 1, blank (B): {{1}} we have arranged to replace it before the cold weather returns.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): The savings from the new boiler's lower gas use {{2}} expected to help keep future rent increases small.
items.hint: (A): Which word shows that the parts belong to the boiler? (B): Is the replacement a result, a contrast, or an example? (C): Find the main noun of the subject. Is it singular or plural?
items.explain:
Blank (A). The parts belong to the boiler, so a possessive is needed. The possessive of it is its, with no apostrophe.

Blank (B). The sentences before it say the boiler broke twice and could not be fixed reliably. Replacing it is the result, so the cause-and-effect transition For this reason, fits.

Blank (C). In “The savings from the new boiler's lower gas use,” the main noun is savings; the rest only describes it. Savings is plural and the notice is in the present tense: “The savings… are expected.” “Is” is the most tempting wrong answer, because it agrees with the nearby word use.

options: its
it's
its'
their
why: “It's” means it is. “Because it is replacement parts are no longer made” makes no sense; you need the possessive.
“Its'” is not a word. The possessive of it never takes an apostrophe.
“Their” is plural, but the parts belong to one thing: the boiler. Use the singular possessive its.

options: For this reason,
However,
For example,
On the other hand,
why: “However” signals a contrast. Replacing the boiler is not in contrast with the breakdowns; it is the result of them.
“For example” introduces an example. Replacing the boiler is not an example of the breakdowns; it is the response to them.
“On the other hand” sets up an opposing point. The replacement follows from the problem, so a cause-and-effect transition is needed.

options: are
is
was
being
why: “Is” is singular. It agrees with the nearby word use, but the subject is savings, which is plural.
“Was” is singular and past tense. The subject savings is plural, and the notice describes a current expectation.
“Being” cannot be the main verb of a sentence. “The savings… being expected” leaves a fragment.

items.prompt:
Complete each statement so that it is supported by the notice.

The notice suggests that management is replacing the boiler in early October, rather than waiting, mainly {{0}}.

The community room will most likely stay open all day on October 6 because {{1}}.

By mentioning that the new boiler uses less gas, the writers most likely hope to {{2}}.
items.hint: For each blank, find the sentence in the notice that the statement depends on, and choose the option you can prove.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Paragraph 1 says the boiler broke down twice last January, leaving residents without heat, and that management will replace it “before the cold weather returns.” The clear inference: they want to prevent another winter breakdown.

Blank 2. From 8:00 a.m. to about 6:00 p.m., apartments will have no heat or hot water. A warm room with coffee gives residents somewhere comfortable to go.

Blank 3. Paragraph 4 follows the bad news with good news: lower gas use and smaller rent increases, then thanks residents for their patience. The writers want residents to see a lasting benefit. The rent-will-go-down choice is the main trap; “keep future rent increases small” does not mean rent will drop.

options: to avoid another heating breakdown once the weather turns cold
because new replacement parts for the old boiler have arrived
because residents complained about the laundry room last winter
because the repair company refuses to work in the winter months
why: This is contradicted. Paragraph 1 says replacement parts “are no longer made,” which is why the boiler cannot be fixed.
This is not supported. The laundry room is mentioned only as closing on October 6; nothing says residents complained about it.
This is not supported. The notice never says when the repair company will or will not work; it says only that the boiler cannot be fixed reliably.

options: residents' apartments will be without heat and hot water most of the day
the crew will use the room as a work space while it installs the boiler
the new boiler will heat only the first floor until it is fully connected
residents will be moving their storage items into the room that day
why: This is not supported. The notice says the crew works on the boiler and the basement storage wall; it never mentions the community room as a work space.
This is outside knowledge or a guess. Nothing in the notice says how the new boiler will heat the building.
This is not supported. Residents are asked to move items away from the back wall of their storage units by Monday, not into the community room.

options: show residents that the disruption will bring a lasting benefit
promise residents that their rent will go down next year
explain why the heat must be shut off for most of October 6
warn residents that gas prices are expected to rise this winter
why: This is overreach. The notice says the savings will help keep rent increases small, not that rent will go down.
This is true but irrelevant. The shutoff is explained in paragraph 2 by the crew's work; the gas savings are about the future.
This is outside knowledge. The notice never mentions gas prices; it mentions using less gas.

items.prompt: Based on the notice, which resident would most likely need to contact the building office by Friday, October 2?
items.hint: Find the sentence in the notice that mentions Friday, October 2. Who does it ask to contact the office?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the request. Paragraph 3 says: “Any resident who has a medical need for hot water on October 6 should contact the office by Friday, October 2.”

Step 2. Apply it. A daily warm-water soak ordered by a doctor is a medical need for hot water, and the hot water will be off on October 6. Correct.

The storage-unit choice is the main trap: that resident does need to act, but the notice asks them to move items by Monday evening, October 5, not to contact the office.
options: a resident whose doctor has ordered a daily soak in warm water
a resident who usually does laundry in the building on Tuesdays
a resident who keeps boxes against the back wall of a storage unit
a resident who works from home and will need heat during the day
why: This resident is affected, but the notice asks nothing of them; they can do laundry on another day. Only residents with a medical need for hot water are asked to contact the office.
This resident must act, but paragraph 2 asks them to move items by Monday evening, not to contact the office.
This resident will lose heat, but the notice asks only residents with a medical need for hot water to contact the office, and it offers the community room to everyone.

items.prompt: In paragraph 10, Mr. Haddad says, “The coffee maker's broken. Fix that and you can stay forever.” What does this remark most likely suggest about him?
items.hint: Has Mr. Haddad praised Teresa directly anywhere in the story? How does he show what he thinks instead?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look at how Mr. Haddad acts. He does not look up when she enters, cuts her off mid-sentence, and slides the key over “without a word.” He never says “good job” or “you're hired.” He shows approval through actions: pocketing her key and handing her the store keys.

Step 2. Read the line for tone. “Stay forever” over a coffee maker is an exaggeration. Right after he gives her the keys, it reads as a joke, a gruff man's way of saying he is pleased.

Step 3. The dry-humor choice is correct. The repair choice is the main trap for readers who take the line literally.
options: He shows approval through dry humor rather than direct praise.
He hired Teresa mainly so that she could repair the store's equipment.
He is irritated that nobody at the store has fixed the coffee maker yet.
He doubts that Teresa will stay at the hardware store for very long.
why: This is overreach. He hired her after she cut a key well; the coffee maker comes up only as a joke after he has already handed her the keys.
This is not supported. Nothing in his words or actions shows irritation; he says it calmly as he goes back to his bolts.
This is contradicted. “Stay forever” and the ring of store keys suggest he expects her to stay.

items.prompt:
Complete each statement so that it is supported by the story.

Mr. Haddad drops the new key into his own shirt pocket most likely because {{0}}.

When Teresa understands that she “would never need to give” her speech, she realizes that {{1}}.

The last sentence, in which Teresa does not check the time for the next bus, suggests that she {{2}}.
items.hint: For each blank, find the action in the story and ask what it shows about the character's thoughts or feelings.
items.explain:
Blank 1. He puts his old key in a drawer and his new key, the one Teresa cut, in his own pocket. Replacing his key with hers shows he trusts her work.

Blank 2. She practiced a speech to win the job, but she was hired because of how she cut the key. Holding the store keys, she realizes the speech is no longer needed.

Blank 3. “For the first time in months, she did not check the time” suggests that for months she had been anxious, watching the clock and the buses. Now, with a job, she feels secure. The walking-home choice is tempting, but the story never says how she leaves.

options: he trusts her work enough to use the key himself
he plans to show the key to Delia later that day
he thinks the key is flawed and wants to check it again
he does not want Teresa to take the key home with her
why: This is not supported. Delia is mentioned only as the person who sent Teresa; nothing links her to the key.
This is contradicted. Right after pocketing it, he puts away the old key and hands Teresa the store keys, which shows he is satisfied.
This is not supported. Nothing suggests Teresa expected to keep the key; the clue is that he replaces his old key with hers.

options: her skill, not her words, has already earned her the job
Mr. Haddad has decided not to hire her after all
she has forgotten the words she practiced on the bus
Delia had already told Mr. Haddad about her speech
why: This is contradicted. She is holding the store keys and has been told she opens on Saturdays.
This misreads the story. The words had “stopped sounding like words,” but she does not need the speech because the job is already hers.
This is not supported. Nothing suggests Delia knew about the speech or told Mr. Haddad anything about it.

options: feels settled and secure for the first time in a while
has decided to walk home instead of taking the bus
plans to buy a car with the money from her new job
missed the bus she needed and will have to wait
why: This is not supported. The story never says how she will get home; the point is that she has stopped worrying.
This is overreach. Nothing mentions a car or her pay; this adds a plan the story never hints at.
This is not supported. The bus passing is not described as her bus, and she is calm, not worried about missing it.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, the author explains that some other records “have gaps of many years” and that “some writers changed their rules for what counted as ‘frozen.’” What is the most likely reason the author includes this information?
items.hint: Read the sentence that comes right after these details. What does Ferro say is “exactly why” Calder Lake's record is valuable?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the details in context. Right after them, the author writes, “Ferro says that is exactly why the Calder Lake record is so valuable,” and Ferro describes it as “the same question, asked the same way, at the same spot, for 140 years.”

Step 2. Gaps and changing rules are the weaknesses of the other records. Paragraph 2 says Calder Lake's record never stopped and its rule never changed. The contrast makes Calder Lake's strengths stand out.

Step 3. The contrast choice is correct. The reliability choice is the main trap if you miss that the weaknesses belong to other records.
options: to show, by contrast, why the steady Calder Lake record is so valuable
to argue that all eleven of the other records should be thrown out
to suggest that Dr. Ferro's findings about Calder Lake may not be reliable
to explain why church diaries are more trustworthy than a mill owner's notes
why: This is overreach. The passage says “not every record is usable,” not that none are, and all goes beyond that.
This is contradicted. The weaknesses belong to the other records; they make the Calder Lake record look stronger, not weaker.
This is not supported. The passage never compares the church diary with the mill owner's notes.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 1, what can the reader infer about why Grace Okafor first asked a neighbor to lend her a ladder?
items.hint: Look at the dollar amount and her quotation in paragraph 1. Then notice the word “Instead.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the clues. The tools would have cost more than $400, and she says, “I was going to use each of them maybe twice a year.” Then the word Instead introduces her note asking to borrow a ladder.

Step 2. Connect them: spending $400 on tools used twice a year is a poor deal, so she looked for another way.

Step 3. The waste-of-money choice matches. Correct. The library choice is the main trap, because the library is the subject of the passage, but paragraph 2 shows the idea came afterward.
options: Buying tools she would rarely use seemed like a waste of money.
She had already planned to start a tool library for the city.
The hardware store near her house had no ladders for sale that week.
She wanted to get to know the people on her new street.
why: This is contradicted. Paragraph 2 says the library idea came later, after two callers asked to borrow something from her.
This is not supported. The passage never says a store was out of ladders; the reason it gives is cost compared with how often she would use them.
This is not supported for that moment. Paragraph 7 talks about neighbors helping each other, but in paragraph 1 her reason is the cost of tools.

items.prompt: The reader can infer that Dale Kessler's worry about the tool library turned out to be mistaken. Click the sentence from paragraph 6 that best supports this inference.
items.hint: One sentence shows what he feared. Which sentence shows what actually happened?
items.explain:
Step 1. The inference is that his worry was mistaken, so the evidence must show what actually happened after the library opened.

Step 2. The first two sentences state the worry. The last sentence offers his explanation.

Step 3. “Instead, he says, his sales… have grown” gives the result: his business did better, not worse. The word Instead signals that the result was the opposite of what he feared. Correct.
spans: Hardware store owner Dale Kessler admits he was worried when the library opened two blocks from his shop.
“I figured nobody would buy a drill again,” he said.
Instead, he says, his sales of screws, paint, lumber, and other supplies have grown, and he now donates a tool to the library every month.
“Somebody who borrows a tile saw still has to buy the tile,” he said.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the tile saw quotation. It explains why borrowers might still shop at his store, but it is a reason, not a result. Only the sentence about his sales growing shows what actually happened to his business.

items.prompt: Based on Paul Medina's statement in paragraph 4, what can the reader infer?
items.hint: What does “showed us” suggest about what the city knew before? Why mention storms “too small to make the news”?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the clues. Medina says the binders showed “exactly which streets flood, even in storms too small to make the news,” and the city then budgeted for new drains on those blocks.

Step 2. Connect them: if the binders showed the city which streets flood, the city did not fully know before. Small floods did not make the news, so they went unreported.

Step 3. The choice saying the city had not known about some of the flooding matches. Correct. The vacuum choice is tempting because the loans and the floods appear together, but the floods came first.
options: The city had not known about some of the flooding on those blocks.
The tool library's loans of wet-dry vacuums caused the flooding there.
Every street in the city floods during even small rainstorms.
Paul Medina often borrows tools from the Fenwick Street library.
why: This reverses cause and effect. People borrowed the vacuums because their streets flooded; the loans did not cause the water.
This is overreach. Medina says the binders showed “which streets flood,” which means some streets do and others do not; the loans clustered on six blocks.
This is not supported. Medina is quoted as a city engineer who studied the binders; nothing says he borrows tools.

items.prompt: Grace Okafor believes that neighbors are willing to help and trust one another. Which two details from the passage best support her view? Select two answers.
items.hint: Look for one detail that shows neighbors offering help and one that shows borrowers keeping their word.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find her view. In paragraph 5 she says people treat the tools “like they belong to a neighbor,” and in paragraph 7 she says the library builds “the habit of asking your neighbors for help.”

Step 2. Look for details that show neighbors helping and trusting. Six callers within a week shows neighbors willing to help a near stranger. Only 4 lost tools out of 4,850 loans shows borrowers can be trusted.

Step 3. Those two are correct. The library's size is the most tempting wrong choice, but growth alone does not prove trust.
options: Six people called within a week after she asked to borrow a ladder.
Of last year's 4,850 loans, only 4 tools never came back at all.
The library now lends more than 1,100 tools, including tile saws.
Volunteers log every loan by hand in a binder.
A council member argued that most borrowers would never return tools.
The city budgeted for new storm drains on four blocks.
why: This shows how large the library has grown, not whether neighbors help or trust each other.
This describes how loans are recorded. It is true but irrelevant to whether neighbors are willing to help.
This is the opposite view: a doubt that borrowers could be trusted. It does not support Okafor's belief.
This is a result of the flood data. It is true but irrelevant to neighbors helping one another.

items.prompt: Use paragraph 5. How many of last year's loans came back on time? Type the number.
items.hint: Two groups did not come back on time. Subtract both from the total.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the numbers in paragraph 5: 4,850 loans; 31 came back late; 4 never came back.

Step 2. Loans not on time: 31 + 4 = 35.

Step 3. On time: 4,850 − 35 = 4,815.

Answer: 4,815. This number is the evidence that answers the council member's worry: nearly every tool came back on time.

mistakes.why: You subtracted only the 31 late tools. The 4 tools that never came back were not on time either: 4,850 − 31 − 4 = 4,815.
You subtracted only the 4 lost tools. The 31 late tools also did not come back on time: 4,850 − 31 − 4 = 4,815.
35 is the number of loans that did not come back on time (31 + 4). The question asks how many did.

items.prompt: In paragraph 7, Okafor tells other towns that “the tools are the easy part.” What does she most likely mean?
items.hint: Read the two sentences that follow her line. What does she say is the real work?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the sentences after the line: “Anybody can collect a shelf of drills… What you're really building is the habit of asking your neighbors for help.”

Step 2. She contrasts the easy part (collecting tools) with the real work (building the habit of asking neighbors for help).

Step 3. So she means the human side is harder and more important. Correct. The “very little work” choice is the main trap: it takes “easy part” and stretches it to the whole project.
options: Getting neighbors to rely on each other is harder and matters more.
Tools are cheap enough now that most people can buy their own.
Other towns already have plenty of spare tools ready to lend.
Starting a tool library takes very little time or hard work.
why: This is contradicted. Paragraph 1 says her tools would have cost more than $400, which is why she borrowed instead.
This is not supported. The passage never describes what tools other towns have.
This stretches her words too far. She says the tools are the easy part, not that the whole project is easy; the next lines name a harder part.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 1 and 4, how does Andre most likely feel as he starts his first morning at the bakery?
items.hint: What did he do the night before, and how does he answer Mrs. Ruiz's first comment?
items.explain:
Step 1. Gather clues. He arrives ten minutes early, set three alarms, and did not need any of them (he barely slept). In paragraph 4 he rushes to explain himself, starting over (“I mean”) and trailing off.

Step 2. Connect them: arriving early and over-preparing show he cares; the nervous, rambling answer shows anxiety.

Step 3. “Anxious and eager to prove himself” fits. Correct. The annoyed choice is tempting because he stands waiting, but he chose to come early.
options: anxious and eager to prove himself
confident because he has baked there before
annoyed that Mrs. Ruiz kept him waiting
unsure whether he wants to be a baker
why: This is contradicted. Mrs. Ruiz knows only that her nephew says he can bake, and Andre admits he has made bread “at home, mostly.”
This is contradicted. Mrs. Ruiz opens “at four exactly”; Andre waits only because he came ten minutes early.
This is contradicted by his preparation. Someone who sets three alarms and arrives early wants to do well.

items.prompt: Mrs. Ruiz never says, “You've got the job.” Which detail best supports the inference that she has decided to keep Andre?
items.hint: Which action changes his status at the bakery?
items.explain:
Step 1. The inference is that she has decided to keep him, so the evidence must show a decision.

Step 2. Smelling the roll is testing; adjusting the oven is helping; looking at his sneakers is a first impression.

Step 3. Crossing out TRIAL and rewriting his name in marker, which is permanent, instead of pencil, shows his place is no longer a trial. Correct.
options: She crosses out TRIAL and rewrites his name underneath in marker.
She breaks one of his rolls in half and smells it at the counter.
She turns the oven dial a quarter turn and moves the rack up a notch.
She looks at his clean white sneakers for a long moment at the door.
why: This shows her checking his work. It comes before any decision, so it does not show that she has decided.
This shows her quietly helping him fix a mistake. Helping during a trial is not the same as deciding to keep him.
This is her first impression of him at the door, before he has baked anything. It is not evidence of a decision.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category based on the story.
items.hint: For each statement, ask: Does the story say this in so many words? If not, do the clues lead there? If not, it is not supported.
items.explain:
Stated directly: “3:50 a.m., ten minutes early” (paragraph 1); “My nephew says you can bake” (paragraph 3).

Reasonable inference: He set three alarms and “had not needed any of them,” so he was already awake before they rang; together with his early arrival, this points to a nervous night. Mrs. Ruiz eats a whole roll from the second tray and then changes his status on the schedule, which shows she was pleased.

Not supported: The story never says how Andre knows the nephew, and pay is never mentioned.
choices: Andre arrived at the bakery ten minutes early.
Mrs. Ruiz's nephew told her that Andre can bake.
Andre was nervous the night before his first shift.
Mrs. Ruiz was pleased with Andre's second tray.
Mrs. Ruiz's nephew is Andre's best friend.
Andre will earn more money now that his trial is over.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting “Andre was nervous the night before” under “Not supported.” The story never says it, but setting three alarms and needing none of them is a strong clue that he was awake and worried before they rang. Another common mistake is calling the nephew Andre's best friend, which is a guess.

items.prompt:
Read the draft notice. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): Employees who usually park in the north lot must move {{0}} cars to the south lot by 10:00 p.m. on Friday, May 15.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): {{1}} the south lot's 140 spaces will not be enough on Monday, when about 210 day-shift employees park on site.

Paragraph 2, blank (C): Each of the two shuttle vans {{2}} room for twelve riders.
items.hint: (A): Who owns the cars? (B): Do the weekend and Monday sentences agree or contrast? (C): Is the subject “Each” or “vans”?
items.explain:
Blank (A). The cars belong to the employees, so a plural possessive is needed: their.

Blank (B). The sentence before says the south lot will have plenty of room on the weekend. This sentence says it will not be enough on Monday. That is a contrast, so However, fits.

Blank (C). The subject is Each; “of the two shuttle vans” only describes it. Each is singular, so the verb is has. “Have” is the most tempting wrong answer because it agrees with the nearby word vans.

options: their
there
they're
its
why: “There” points to a place (“over there”). The cars belong to the employees, so you need the possessive their.
“They're” means they are. “Must move they are cars” makes no sense.
“Its” is singular. The owners are employees, which is plural, so use their.

options: However,
For this reason,
For example,
In addition,
why: “For this reason” signals a result. The weekend having plenty of room does not cause Monday to be short; the two ideas contrast.
“For example” introduces an example of the sentence before. A shortage on Monday is not an example of plenty of room on the weekend.
“In addition” adds a similar point. Monday's shortage is the opposite of the weekend's extra room, so a contrast word is needed.

options: has
have
having
were
why: “Have” is plural. It agrees with the nearby word vans, but the subject is Each, which is singular.
“Having” cannot be the main verb. “Each of the two shuttle vans having room” is a fragment.
“Were” is plural and past tense. The subject Each is singular, and the notice describes the vans in the present tense.

items.prompt:
Complete each statement so that it is supported by the notice.

The notice suggests that the company decided to repave the north lot mainly because {{0}}.

The company most likely rented the church lot because {{1}}.

Giving carpoolers first choice of south-lot spaces is most likely meant to {{2}}.
items.hint: For blank 2, compare the number of employees with the number of spaces. For the others, find the sentence each statement depends on.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Paragraph 1 opens with deep potholes and two employees with tire damage. That is the problem the repaving solves.

Blank 2. About 210 employees park on Monday, and the south lot has 140 spaces: 210 − 140 = 70 employees without a space. The church lot is rented “to make up the difference.”

Blank 3. Each carpool puts several employees in one car, so fewer spaces are needed. Rewarding carpoolers with the closest lot encourages that. The “about 70 new employees” option in blank 1 is a trap built from the same numbers used in blank 2.

options: the potholes had become a safety and repair problem for employees
the church on Carver Road asked the company to stop using its lot
the company is hiring about 70 new day-shift employees this spring
the lights along the east edge of the lot had stopped working
why: This is not supported. The company is renting the church lot for Monday; nothing says it had used it before or was asked to stop.
This misreads the numbers. About 70 is the gap between 210 employees and 140 spaces, not a number of new hires.
This is not supported. The four new lights are an improvement in the repaved lot; the notice never says old lights failed.

options: about 70 day-shift employees would have no place to park on Monday
the church lot is closer to the building than the south lot is
the south lot is also being repaved during the same three days
weekend workers asked for more parking spaces near the building
why: This is contradicted. The church lot is “about a mile away,” which is why shuttle vans are needed.
This is contradicted. The notice tells employees to move their cars to the south lot, so it is not being repaved.
This is contradicted. The notice says the south lot will have “plenty of room” on the weekend.

options: reduce the number of cars that need a space on Monday
reward the employees who arrive at work the earliest
punish employees who leave cars in the north lot
free up seats in the shuttle vans for visitors
why: This is not supported. The notice ties first choice to carpooling, not to arrival time.
This is not supported. Cars left in the north lot are towed; carpooling is a separate, voluntary choice.
This is not supported. The vans are for employees parking at the church lot; visitors are never mentioned.

items.prompt: Based on the notice, which employee would most likely need to contact a supervisor by Wednesday, May 13?
items.hint: Find the sentence in the notice that mentions Wednesday, May 13. Who does it ask to contact a supervisor?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the request. Paragraph 3 says: “If you plan to carpool, please tell your supervisor by Wednesday, May 13.”

Step 2. Apply it. Driving two coworkers to work on Monday is carpooling. Correct.

The north-lot choice is the main trap: that employee does need to act, but the notice asks them to move their car by 10:00 p.m. on Friday, May 15, not to contact a supervisor.
options: an employee who plans to drive two coworkers to work on Monday
an employee who usually parks in the north lot on weekday mornings
an employee who works only on Saturdays in the warehouse
an employee who rides the city bus to work every day
why: This employee must act, but paragraph 1 asks them to move their car by Friday night, not to contact a supervisor.
This employee works on a day when the south lot has plenty of room, and the notice asks nothing of weekend workers.
This employee does not park on site, so the parking changes do not require any action from them.

items.prompt: In paragraph 8, Mrs. Ruiz says, “Burn another one, and you're eating it for lunch.” What does this remark most likely suggest about her?
items.hint: What has she just done with the schedule? How does that change the way you hear her words?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look at what she does right before the line: she eats a whole roll from his second tray, crosses out TRIAL, and rewrites his name in marker.

Step 2. Read the line for tone. “You're eating it for lunch” is a mock threat, said “already turning away.” It assumes he will be there tomorrow, burning or not burning trays.

Step 3. The gruff-teasing choice is correct. The angry choice is the main trap for readers who take the words literally and ignore her actions.
options: She is truly angry that Andre wasted a tray of conchas.
She shows that she has accepted him through gruff teasing.
She plans to make Andre pay for the rolls he ruined.
She doubts that Andre will last long at the bakery.
why: This is contradicted. She calmly sends the first tray to the church pantry and has just eaten a whole roll from his second tray.
This takes the joke literally and stretches it. The first tray goes to the church pantry; nothing says Andre must pay.
This is contradicted. She has just crossed out TRIAL and written his name in marker, which signals he is staying.

items.prompt:
Complete each statement so that it is supported by the story.

Mrs. Ruiz turns the oven dial and moves the rack most likely because {{0}}.

Rewriting Andre's name in marker instead of pencil suggests that {{1}}.

The last sentence, in which Andre does not brush the flour off his sneakers, suggests that he {{2}}.
items.hint: For blank 3, look back at paragraph 2. What did Mrs. Ruiz notice about his sneakers then?
items.explain:
Blank 1. His first tray comes out pale on top and dark on the bottom. She silently adjusts the heat and the rack, then lets him try again. She is fixing the problem without a lecture.

Blank 2. Pencil can be erased; marker cannot. Crossing out TRIAL and rewriting his name in marker shows his place is no longer temporary.

Blank 3. In paragraph 2, Mrs. Ruiz stares at his clean white sneakers, the mark of a newcomer. Now they are white with flour, like her forearms, and he leaves the flour on: he is proud to look like he belongs. The tired choice is tempting because he started early, but the story connects the moment to his new place, not to fatigue.

options: she sees what went wrong with his first tray and quietly fixes it
she needs the oven at a different heat for her own baking
the oven is broken and must be adjusted by hand every hour
she has decided to finish baking the conchas herself
why: This is not supported. She adjusts the oven right after his tray comes out uneven and then goes back to her own work.
This is not supported. Nothing says the oven is broken; the adjustment follows his badly baked tray.
This is contradicted. She goes back to her own work, and Andre bakes the second tray himself.

options: his place at the bakery is now permanent rather than temporary
the pencil had faded and was getting hard to read
she had spelled his name wrong the first time
she wants the schedule to be easier to see from the cooler
why: This takes the action literally. Nothing says the pencil had faded; the change comes right after she crosses out TRIAL.
This is not supported. She writes “Andre” again, the same name, so nothing suggests a spelling error.
This is not supported. Readability is never mentioned; the meaningful change is from TRIAL in pencil to his name in marker.

options: is proud to look like he belongs in the bakery now
is too tired from the early start to clean his shoes
has stopped caring about how he looks at work
plans to quit as soon as his shift is over
why: This is not supported. Nothing suggests he is too tired; the moment comes right after he earns his place.
This is overreach. Keeping the flour on is a choice that shows pride, not a general loss of care.
This is contradicted. He has just been taken off trial and seems glad about it.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author reports that a council member “argued that most borrowers would never return the tools.” What is the most likely reason the author includes this information?
items.hint: Read the sentence that comes right after the council member's argument. What does it say the records do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the detail in context. Right after it, the author writes, “The library's records answer that worry,” and gives the numbers: 4,850 loans, 31 late, 4 never returned.

Step 2. The council member's argument is a doubt; the numbers show the doubt was wrong.

Step 3. The set-up-a-doubt choice is correct. The poorly organized choice is the main trap if you stop reading at the council member's argument.
options: to argue that borrowers who return tools late should have to pay fines
to suggest that the tool library is poorly organized and hard to manage
to set up an early doubt that the library's records then show was wrong
to explain why the city later paid for new storm drains on four blocks
why: This is not supported. The passage never suggests fines; the library “still charges nothing.”
This is contradicted. The records show almost every tool came back, which suggests the library is well run.
This is true but irrelevant to paragraph 5. The storm drains come from the flood data in paragraph 4.

stimuli.title: When the Fines Stopped
stimuli.html:
[1] For decades, the Brookfield Public Library charged ten cents a day for every overdue book. In 2019, the library board voted to end the fines. Some residents objected. “If there's no penalty, why would anyone bring books back?” one man asked at the meeting.

[2] The library's director, Helen Achebe, had studied the numbers before the vote. Fines brought in about $14,000 a year, less than one percent of the library's budget. Meanwhile, about 2,300 residents had library cards that were blocked because they owed more than $10. Nearly half of those blocked cards belonged to children and teenagers.

[3] In the year after fines ended, the library sent the same reminder emails it always had, and it still charged for lost books. The share of books returned within a month of the due date rose slightly, from 94 percent to 95 percent. About 1,100 residents whose cards had been blocked came back and borrowed again.

[4] Some of the returning borrowers left notes in the book drop. One, written in pencil on the back of a receipt, said, “Sorry this took two years. Thank you for letting me come back.” Achebe keeps it pinned above her desk.

[5] Staff noticed another change. Before, the circulation desk spent part of nearly every shift arguing with patrons over small amounts of money. “Now those conversations are about what people want to read next,” said Marco Liu, who has worked at the desk for nine years.

stimuli.title: The Recital
stimuli.html:
An original short story.

[1] Mina's father came to the school auditorium straight from the job site, still in his orange safety vest and dusty boots, and took a seat in the back row. When the fourth-grade choir filed onto the stage, Mina searched the rows of faces until she found him. Then she looked down at her shoes and did not look up again for the whole first song.

[2] Afterward, in the crowded hallway, he held out a small bunch of grocery-store daisies still wrapped in plastic. Mina took them without a word and walked a step ahead of him to the truck. Halfway home, at a red light, she said quietly, “Next time you could change first.” He nodded and kept his eyes on the road.

[3] When they got home, Mina carried the daisies inside, filled a glass with water, and set them on her windowsill, where she would see them first thing when she woke up.

stimuli.title: Late Hours at the Riverside Rec Center
stimuli.html:
[1] For years, the Riverside Recreation Center closed at 6 p.m. on weeknights. In 2022, the city began keeping the gym and computer room open until 10 p.m. for teenagers and young adults. Some neighbors objected. “You're just inviting trouble after dark,” one said at a public meeting.

[2] The center's manager, Luis Ferreira, had studied the numbers before the change. Staying open four more hours would cost about $38,000 a year, mostly to pay two staff members. Meanwhile, police records showed that most calls about teenagers in the neighborhood came between 6 and 10 p.m., when the center was closed and the nearest library had shut too.

[3] In the first year of late hours, the center counted about 160 visitors a night after 6 p.m. Calls to police about teenagers in the neighborhood during those hours fell from 410 the year before to 230. Staff reported two minor scuffles inside the building all year, and both were broken up within minutes.

[4] Some regular visitors started helping out. A group of older teens now runs a Thursday basketball league for younger kids, and two of them were hired as part-time staff this spring.

[5] The change has affected the staff, too. “I used to spend my afternoons chasing kids out of the parking lot,” said Gloria Banks, who has worked at the front desk for eleven years. “Now I spend my evenings learning their names.”

stimuli.title: The 6:10
stimuli.html:
An original short story.

[1] Ray had driven the 6:10 bus for twenty-two years. On his last morning, he pulled up to the stop at Elm and Fifth and saw Mrs. Albee waiting in her blue raincoat, though the sky was clear. She climbed the steps slowly, paid in exact change, and sat in the first seat behind him, where she had sat for as long as he could remember.

[2] She did not say goodbye when they reached her stop. She stood, buttoned her raincoat, and pressed a small paper bag into his hand without looking at him. Then she stepped down to the curb and walked away faster than he had ever seen her walk.

[3] At the end of the line, Ray opened the bag. Inside were two oatmeal cookies, still warm, and an index card that said, in shaky capital letters, 6:10 WON'T BE THE SAME.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 2, what can the reader infer about why Helen Achebe supported ending fines?
items.explain: Clues in paragraph 2: fines brought in less than one percent of the budget, while about 2,300 residents, nearly half of them young people, had blocked cards. Connect: fines cost the library little to give up but kept many people from borrowing. That is the most likely reason she supported ending them. The “never return books” choice is tempting because a resident raised that worry in paragraph 1, but it was his worry, not her reason.
options: She wanted the library to raise more money each year from overdue books.
She saw that fines kept many people from the library and earned little.
She believed that most borrowers would never return their books anyway.
She had been ordered by the city to cut the library's operating costs.
why: This is contradicted. Ending fines meant giving up about $14,000 a year, so it could not raise money.
This is not supported. Paragraph 2 says nothing about borrowers failing to return books; the numbers she studied were about income and blocked cards.
This is not supported. No city order is mentioned; the passage says she studied the numbers herself.

items.prompt: The reader can infer that ending fines did not cause people to stop returning books. Click the sentence that best supports this inference.
items.explain: The inference is about whether people kept returning books, so the best evidence must measure returns. The return rate rose from 94 to 95 percent: returns did not fall; they went up slightly. The man's question states the opposite worry, the 1,100 sentence is about borrowing, and the receipt note describes one person's very late return.
spans: “If there's no penalty, why would anyone bring books back?” one man asked at the meeting.
In the year after fines ended, the library sent the same reminder emails it always had, and it still charged for lost books.
The share of books returned within a month of the due date rose slightly, from 94 percent to 95 percent.
About 1,100 residents whose cards had been blocked came back and borrowed again.
One, written in pencil on the back of a receipt, said, “Sorry this took two years. Thank you for letting me come back.”
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about reminder emails and lost-book charges. It describes what the library still did, but not what borrowers actually did. Only the return-rate sentence measures whether books kept coming back.

items.prompt: Which two inferences are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
items.explain: Choice 1: about 2,300 cards were blocked for unpaid fines, about 1,100 of those residents came back once fines ended, and a note thanks the library “for letting me come back.” Choice 2: Marco Liu says desk conversations used to be arguments over money and are now about what people want to read. The $14,000 choice is the most tempting wrong answer, but it turns lost income into savings.
options: Some residents had stopped using the library because of money they owed.
Desk staff now spend less time in disputes with patrons over money.
Ending fines saved the library about $14,000 in its first year.
Every resident with a blocked card came back to the library.
Most libraries in the country have now stopped charging fines.
why: This misreads the numbers. The $14,000 was money the fines brought in; ending them meant losing that income, not saving it.
This is overreach. About 1,100 of about 2,300 blocked residents came back, which is fewer than half.
This is outside knowledge. The passage is about one library and never discusses libraries across the country.

items.prompt: Use paragraphs 2 and 3. About how many residents with blocked cards did not come back to borrow in the year after fines ended? Type the number.
items.explain: Paragraph 2: about 2,300 residents had blocked cards. Paragraph 3: about 1,100 of them came back and borrowed again. Those who did not come back: 2,300 − 1,100 = 1,200. This is why “every resident with a blocked card came back” would be overreach.

mistakes.why: 1,100 is the number who did come back. Subtract it from the 2,300 blocked residents: 2,300 − 1,100 = 1,200.
2,300 is the total number of blocked cards. Some of those residents came back, so subtract the 1,100 who did.
You added the two numbers. The question asks how many did not come back, so subtract: 2,300 − 1,100 = 1,200.

items.prompt: Which conclusion goes beyond what the passage supports?
items.explain: The return rate rose only slightly, from 94 to 95 percent. That shows returns did not drop; it does not show residents became “far more careful.” That conclusion is overreach. Each of the other three can be proved with a specific line from the passage.
options: Without fines, residents became far more careful about returning books on time.
Fines made up only a small part of the money the library spent each year.
At least one borrower felt grateful to be allowed to use the library again.
The library still had a way to recover the cost of books that were lost.
why: This is supported. Paragraph 2 says fines were less than one percent of the library's budget.
This is supported. The note in paragraph 4 says, “Thank you for letting me come back.”
This is supported. Paragraph 3 says the library “still charged for lost books.”

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 1, how does Mina most likely feel when she sees her father in the audience?
items.explain: Mina looks down right after she finds her father and does not look up for the whole song. The clue about why comes in paragraph 2: “Next time you could change first.” His orange vest and dusty boots embarrassed her. The proud choice is the main trap, since he did come straight from work, but her actions show embarrassment, not pride.
options: embarrassed by the way he is dressed
angry that he arrived late to the show
proud that he came straight from work
afraid she will forget the song's words
why: This is not supported. Nothing says he was late; he took a seat before the choir came on stage.

This is not supported. Nothing mentions the words of the song; she looks down only after she finds her father.

items.prompt: What does paragraph 3 most likely suggest about Mina?
items.explain: Mina took the daisies “without a word” and asked her father to change next time, but at home she puts them in water and places them where she will see them “first thing when she woke up.” That careful action shows the gift matters to her. Her feelings are mixed: embarrassment at the recital, and love for her father. The angry choice is tempting if you stop reading at paragraph 2.
options: She plans to give the daisies to her teacher at school the next morning.
She is still too angry with her father to forgive him for coming.
She values her father's gift even though she was embarrassed earlier.
She likes daisies better than any other kind of flower she knows.
why: This is not supported. She sets them on her own windowsill, where she will see them when she wakes up.
This is contradicted. Putting his flowers in water where she will see them first thing shows care, not anger.
This is outside the text. Nothing compares daisies with other flowers; the point is who gave them to her.

items.prompt: The reader can infer that keeping the center open late did not bring the trouble some neighbors feared. Click the sentence that best supports this inference.

items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about police records in paragraph 2. It is about trouble, but it describes the time before the change. Only the drop from 410 to 230 calls shows what happened after the center stayed open.

items.prompt: Which two inferences are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
items.explain: Choice 1: the center and the nearest library were both closed from 6 to 10 p.m. Choice 2: older teens run a basketball league for younger kids, and two were hired as part-time staff. options: Before the change, many teens had few places to go on weeknight evenings.

Every regular teen visitor has been hired by the center.
why: This is not supported. The passage gives the $38,000 cost but never says any savings made up for it.

items.prompt: Use paragraph 3. By how many did police calls about teenagers in the neighborhood fall in the first year of late hours? Type the number.
items.explain: Paragraph 3: calls fell from 410 the year before to 230. The drop is 410 − 230 = 180. Since 230 calls still came in, “the late hours ended all trouble” would be overreach.

vocab.def: A logical conclusion a reader reaches by combining clues in a text with everyday knowledge.
vocab.example: Wet shoes and a dripping umbrella lead to the inference that it is raining.

vocab.def: To figure out something that the text suggests but does not say directly. Readers infer.
vocab.example: From her shaking hands, I infer that she is nervous.

vocab.def: To suggest an idea without saying it directly. Writers and speakers imply.
vocab.example: By saying “We are hiring,” the sign implies the café needs workers.

vocab.def: Stated clearly and directly in the text.
vocab.example: “Dana was angry” states her feeling explicitly.

vocab.def: Suggested by clues but not stated directly.
vocab.example: Dana's anger is implicit in “She slammed the door.”

vocab.def: Specific words, facts, or quotations from a text that support an answer or claim.
vocab.example: “Ninety people were still on the waiting list” is textual evidence of high demand.

vocab.def: To point to or quote the exact part of a text that supports your answer.
vocab.example: Cite paragraph 4 to show that the ice now goes out earlier.

vocab.def: A detail in a text that helps the reader figure out something that is not stated.
vocab.example: Balloons and wrapping paper are clues that a party took place.

vocab.def: A judgment or decision reached by reasoning from evidence.
vocab.example: The shelf was a success, since the owner added a second one.

vocab.def: Backed up by evidence in the text; a supported answer can be proved by pointing to specific words.
vocab.example: “The pool is short on lifeguards” is supported by the canceled lap swim.

vocab.def: An answer that goes further than the evidence allows, often using words like all, never, always, or only.
vocab.example: “Everyone in town loves the park” overreaches if only three people are quoted.

vocab.def: The ways an author shows what a character is like, through speech, actions, thoughts, and others' reactions.
vocab.example: A boss who hands a new worker the store keys without a word shows trust.

vocab.def: A two-part GED question: the first asks for an inference, and the second asks which evidence best supports it.
vocab.example: Part A: What does the narrator suggest? Part B: Which sentence supports your answer?

vocab.def: A check for any inference or answer choice: point to the exact words in the text that support it. If you cannot, cross the choice out.
vocab.example: “The café is short on workers” passes the prove-it test: the same sign says “We are hiring!”

vocab.def: An answer trap: a real detail from the text that does not answer the question being asked.
vocab.example: “The clinic meets in the library basement” is true but does not show that the clinic meets a need.

notes:
Week 2 RLA Study Sheet: Inference and Textual Evidence

Key terms

  • Explicit: stated directly
  • Implicit: suggested by clues
  • Imply: what the writer does (hints)
  • Infer: what the reader does (figures out)
  • Inference: a conclusion supported by text clues
  • Textual evidence: exact words or facts that prove an answer

The formula

Text clues + what I know = inference

Clues come from the text. What you know only connects them.

Four steps

  1. Read the question; note what it asks about.
  2. Go back to the text; mark the clues.
  3. Make your own inference first.
  4. Prove it: point to the words.

Best evidence checklist

  • Relevant: about the exact idea
  • Specific: fact, number, action, or quote
  • Direct: if it is true, the idea must be true

Character clues

  • What the character says
  • What the character does
  • What the character thinks
  • How others react

People do not always mean exactly what they say. Read jokes and short answers for tone.

Prove-it test: If you cannot point to the words that support a choice, cross it out.

Answer traps

TrapSignAsk yourself
OverreachAll, never, always, only, provesDo the clues really go this far?
Outside knowledgeTrue in life, missing from the textCould I reach this from the passage alone?
ContradictedThe opposite of what the text showsDoes any line say otherwise?
True but irrelevantA real detail that does not answer the questionDoes this answer what was asked?

Paired questions (Part A and Part B)

  1. Answer Part A and put your cursor on the line that led you there.
  2. For Part B, look for that line first.
  3. Check: if this detail is true, must the Part A answer be true?

Question wording to recognize

“It can be inferred…” • “The author suggests…” • “most likely” • “Which detail best supports…?” • “Click the sentence that best supports…” • “What does the speaker most likely mean?” • “Why does the author include…?”

Strategy: Prove it before you pick it. Predict the inference in your own words, match it to a choice, and point to the words that prove it. Name the trap on every choice you cut.
